A controlled teacher swap between Math-RL and Code-RL reverses the relative effectiveness of math and code supports across four evaluations, with the student and supports held fixed. Selection is not reliably better than random sampling: uniform random support selection is competitive or best in several comparisons, and excluding GSM8K from a mixed pool does not consistently improve results.10c:T8bb,方法核心是 Interactive-Policy Distillation, IPD。它不是让学生完整生成、教师事后打分，也不是让教师始终主导轨迹，而是设计了一个 bidirectional propose-and-verify 状态机。学生和教师轮流扮演 proposer 与 verifier：当前 proposer 生成若干 token，verifier 判断当前前缀是否仍处在可接受区域；如果学生轨迹开始漂移，教师接管并给出一段纠偏 continuation；当轨迹重新回到学生能够承接的区域，再把控制权交还给学生。这样得到的训练样本是 mixed-source trajectory，其中一部分 token 来自学生，一部分来自教师。

在损失设计上，作者没有对整条混合轨迹统一套一个 KL，而是按 token 来源拆开。对学生自己提出的 token 位置，用 reverse KL，让学生在自己访问到的状态上向教师分布靠拢，但不过度覆盖教师所有 mode；这更接近 on-policy distillation 的目标，也更适合小模型在自身可实现的解空间里收缩分布。对教师接管时生成的 token 位置，用 forward KL，让学生直接模仿教师纠偏后的 continuation；这部分更像局部离线蒸馏。这个 source-split objective 是论文最有方法含量的地方，因为它把 on-policy 和 off-policy 蒸馏拼接在同一条轨迹里，而不是简单做数据级混合。

工程上，作者还实现了 fused inference engine，把 teacher 和 student 共置于一个 serving instance，分别维护 KV cache，并根据当前 proposer/verifier 角色调度请求。这个系统细节不是论文主创新，但它解决了双模型交替 rollout 的实际开销问题，否则 IPD 很容易因为 teacher intervention 过于频繁而失去训练效率。

和已有 OPD 的区别主要有三点。第一，传统 OPD 默认学生轨迹始终可被教师稳定评估，IPD 明确承认并处理 unanchoring。第二，已有方法常在样本级混合 on-policy/off-policy 数据，IPD 在 token 级别区分 supervision。第三，教师不是静态 labeler，而是交互式纠偏者。这个设计更像 DAgger 在语言模型蒸馏场景下的细化版本，但作者把它落到了 token-level KL 训练上，而不是只做行为克隆。10d:T952,The core method is Interactive-Policy Distillation, or IPD. Instead of letting the student generate a full trajectory and querying the teacher afterward, or letting the teacher dominate the whole rollout, IPD uses a bidirectional propose-and-verify state machine. Student and teacher alternate between proposer and verifier roles. The current proposer emits tokens, and the verifier checks whether the trajectory remains within an acceptable region. If the student starts to drift, the teacher takes over and provides a corrective continuation. Once the trajectory returns to a region the student can plausibly continue from, control is handed back to the student. The resulting training sample is therefore a mixed-source trajectory, with some tokens proposed by the student and others by the teacher.

The loss is the most interesting part. Rather than applying one KL objective to the entire mixed trajectory, the paper splits supervision by token source. On student-generated positions, it uses reverse KL, which is more aligned with on-policy distillation: the student is trained on states it actually visits and is encouraged to concentrate on realizable modes instead of covering every teacher mode. On teacher-generated positions, it uses forward KL, effectively imitating the teacher’s corrective continuation. This source-split objective is the main methodological contribution because it combines on-policy and off-policy distillation within the same trajectory at token granularity, not just by mixing datasets.

The paper also includes a fused inference engine that co-hosts teacher and student in one serving instance, keeps separate KV caches, and schedules requests according to the current proposer/verifier roles. This is not the conceptual core, but it matters in practice because frequent teacher intervention would otherwise make rollout expensive.

Relative to prior OPD work, the differences are clear. Standard OPD assumes teacher supervision remains meaningful on student rollouts; IPD explicitly handles the case where that assumption breaks. Prior methods often mix on-policy and off-policy data at the sample level; IPD distinguishes them at the token level. And the teacher is not just a static labeler, but an interactive corrector. The overall flavor is reminiscent of DAgger-style correction, but adapted to token-level KL training for language models.10e:T683,The experiments focus on mathematical reasoning distillation across four teacher-student pairs. The main metrics are benchmark-averaged mean@8 and best@8 accuracy. The headline result is that IPD achieves the best average performance and leads on most individual benchmarks. The most concrete number given in the paper summary is on Qwen3-30B-A3B to Qwen3-1.7B-Base distillation: IPD surpasses the mean@8 of OPD trained for a full epoch, 279 steps, after only 60 training steps. That is a strong data-efficiency result.

The experimental story appears to support three claims. First, the gain is not merely from adding more teacher tokens, but from intervening when the student drifts, re-anchoring the trajectory, and then returning control. Second, the source-split objective matters because student-origin and teacher-origin tokens play different roles and should not share one uniform divergence. Third, the method is reasonably robust across training datasets rather than tied to one specific reasoning corpus.

The provided full-text excerpt does not include all tables, but the paper likely contains ablations along the following lines: teacher intervention without source-split loss, source-split loss without interactive takeover, different intervention frequencies or acceptance criteria, and comparisons against pure SFT, pure OPD, and possibly RLVR-style baselines. Those ablations are important because IPD introduces multiple moving parts, and the main question is which component contributes most.

Overall, the empirical contribution is best understood as making OPD more stable and sample-efficient, not as replacing the distillation paradigm itself.10f:T594,A good skim path is: problem definition, state machine, loss, then efficiency results. Start with the Introduction to understand teacher unanchoring and why naive OPD can fail for strong-teacher and weak-student pairs. Then read the methodology figure for the bidirectional propose-and-verify process and make sure it is clear when the teacher takes over and when the student resumes. Next, focus on the source-split objective and the rationale for reverse KL on student tokens versus forward KL on teacher tokens. Finally, inspect the main benchmark table and the training-step comparison curves to see whether the method really improves data efficiency over OPD.

For a skim, 20 to 30 minutes should be enough. Prioritize the method diagram, the main result table, the step-efficiency plots, and the ablation table. For deeper reading, check how the acceptance region is defined, whether it depends on heuristic thresholds, how often teacher intervention happens in practice, and how much throughput the fused engine actually recovers. Those details determine whether the method is suitable for large-scale post-training pipelines.

A longer-term question worth keeping in mind is whether IPD is only useful for small-model reasoning distillation or whether the same framework could be adapted to online teacher shaping earlier in the training stack. The paper does not fully answer that, but it provides a plausible template.110:T455,ABC, or Advantage-Based Control Variates, reformulates trajectory-level control variates using learned advantage and value functions. Standard PPO often relies on TD-style advantage estimates, where value approximation error can bias the update. GRPO removes the learned critic and instead normalizes returns within groups of rollouts. ABC takes a different route: it inserts learned advantage and value terms as control variates for the policy-gradient estimator while preserving unbiasedness. The paper characterizes the covariance of this estimator and relates it to the return decomposition used in Direct Advantage Estimation. It then combines ABC with DAE into an actor-critic algorithm. The critic is first trained on offline data to approximate the advantage and value functions of the target policy, and actor and critic are then updated with online sampled trajectories. The theory shows that the true advantage and value functions minimize the covariance; in deterministic environments, the excess variance can be bounded by return prediction error from the estimated advantage-value decomposition.111:T40a,The paper first compares two forward passes of the same policy over the same sampled response: one with the normal context and one augmented with a hindsight skill written after the trajectory. The skill makes the policy a better actor, but produces little change in next-token distributions. It instead changes hidden states across many response tokens. PR-OPD uses this observation directly. After a GRPO warm start, the policy continues on-policy RL. For each completed trajectory, the model writes a hindsight skill, then re-reads its own sampled response with that skill as a stop-gradient privileged teacher. The student processes the same response without the skill. Instead of matching teacher logits, the student hidden states are passed through lightweight per-layer MLP projectors and aligned to the teacher hidden states across layers. The policy, hindsight analyzer, and teacher share the same weights; the only added module is the projector, and there is no extra teacher model, skill library, or inference-time context.112:T4bf,REVO is an off-policy distillation framework that performs multiple learner updates per student rollout. The base objective is token-level reverse KL between the student and teacher next-token distributions at student-generated prefixes. Naive reuse has two mismatches. Prefix mismatch comes from using prefixes generated by an older student; REVO handles it with geometrically normalized and capped prefix weights to avoid high-variance products of likelihood ratios over long prefixes. Current-token mismatch comes from keeping tokens sampled by an older student; REVO replaces them with one-step resampling from the current student at the stored prefix, avoiding full trajectory regeneration. The second component is variance-guided token prioritization. REVO estimates the variance of the student-teacher log-probability ratio and uses it as a bounded weight for token-level updates. Under a local realizability condition, this variance equals the inner product between the ordinary gradient and the natural gradient of the local reverse-KL objective, linking it to local natural-gradient progress. Empirical diagnostics further connect it to the signal-to-noise ratio of finite-sample logit-gradient estimates.113:T748,The method has two layers. The first is CaRE-Divergence, a token-level objective that interpolates between Forward KL and Reverse KL based on relative confidence. Confidence is measured by normalized entropy from a single forward pass: sharper distributions imply higher confidence. When the teacher is more confident than the student, the gate moves toward Forward KL, encouraging support coverage. When the teacher is less confident, the gate moves toward Reverse KL, making the update more mode-seeking and less sensitive to the teacher’s unreliable tail. The paper considers both hard and sigmoid-based soft gates, but the key idea is that the gate depends on the teacher-student confidence gap rather than a fixed global coefficient.

The second component is Revival, a sequence-level rejection rule. The authors argue that single-pass entropy only captures aleatoric uncertainty and cannot separate intrinsic ambiguity from hallucination-like epistemic uncertainty. To address this, they estimate BALD scores for both teacher and student using Monte Carlo dropout, then reject a distillation update when the teacher is epistemically less reliable than the student. The threshold is defined by running quantiles rather than a fixed scalar, which makes the rule robust to training-time drift in BALD magnitudes.

What distinguishes the paper from prior work is the combination of token-level geometry adaptation and sequence-level supervision rejection. Earlier methods mostly use a static divergence with a global precision-recall bias, or perform filtering at the dataset level. The gradient analysis is also important: the authors argue that no single static divergence can reproduce the conditional behavior of their objective, because a fixed geometry cannot be mean-seeking on some tokens and mode-seeking on others within the same training trajectory.114:T516,The evaluation spans 8 teacher-student pairs and 11 benchmarks covering instruction following, chat alignment, code generation, math reasoning, and factuality. The headline numbers reported in the paper are: +2.6 average ROUGE-L over Forward KL for GPT2-base students, +3.2 for OPT-125M, +2.1 pass@1 on MBPP, +1.7 accuracy on GSM8K, and up to +2.5 per task on LLM-as-a-judge factuality relative to Skewed-RKL. An important result is that Revival is not tied to CaRE-Divergence alone; when added to Forward KL, Reverse KL, alpha-beta divergence, and Skewed RKL, it consistently improves performance. That suggests the sequence-level rejection mechanism is a fairly general enhancement.

The more informative evidence is in the analysis. Figure 1 reportedly shows the Fidelity Trap clearly: when the teacher is accurate, distillation helps by around 4% median gain, but when the teacher is uncertain about its own generation, the gain collapses to roughly 0.5%. The point is not simply that weak teachers hurt; it is that the student is often already better calibrated in those regions and still gets dragged toward unreliable supervision. If the full paper includes bucketed results by confidence gap, gate statistics, and BALD-threshold sensitivity, those are more diagnostic than the aggregate scores.115:T496,The main comparison fixes the same subset of poisoned rows and applies three conditions: leave the mixture untouched, delete the selected rows, or rewrite their completions into correct task-preserving answers for the same prompts. The primary setup follows the bad-medical-advice organism from Turner et al. 2025: Qwen2.5-14B-Instruct with a rank-1 LoRA adapter on the layer-24 down-projection, rsLoRA with α=512, effective batch size 16, learning rate 2e-5, a linear schedule, five warmup steps, and response-only loss. Thinking-mode distillation runs for 142 steps; the non-thinking route runs for 212 steps. Training uses 13,597 DAPO-Math-17k problems with batch size 128. Distillation improves single-sample solving at every student size, but the gains hit two ceilings: the student's own pre-training multi-sample reach and the teacher's performance. A distilled single attempt behaves like a small number of attempts from the starting student, rather than expanding the set of problems the student can solve at all. In thinking mode, stopping fails for smaller students. With the external-SFT start, students quickly stop closing their reasoning blocks and fill the length budget. Along these run-on traces, the teacher gives little signal to stop. Training then acts as a filter: stops that land on correct answers survive, while stops at wrong points are removed. The 4B student sometimes stops at useful points, with roughly half of its stops correct before distillation; the 0.6B student almost never stops at a correct point, so distillation leaves it with almost no stopping behavior. Analysis of non-stopping samples shows that the 0.6B student often reaches the correct value early, more often than chance, but continues writing past it. With teacher-SFT starts, small students mark answers more often but may still overwrite correct ones as generation continues.118:T49f,The main evaluation uses 537 human-authored multi-turn jailbreak conversations and 2,000 WildChat benign conversations sampled to match the attack set’s turn-length distribution. With synthetic benign conversations, a three-turn window reaches 0.98 ROC-AUC. Against realistic WildChat benign traffic, ROC-AUC drops to 0.76, and thresholds selected on synthetic benign data flag more than 90% of real benign conversations. On realistic benign data, the single-turn baseline performs best overall, followed by a two-turn window; longer windows and full-history accumulation reduce separability. The paper attributes this to gradient dilution: benign or unrelated turns add gradient noise and pull the signal away from the unsafe direction. Generalization is also weak. On 200 HarmBench objectives, Crescendo produces 149 confirmed successful attacks, a 74.5% attack success rate, but the gradient detector approaches random behavior on short windows and can rank successful attacks below benign conversations on longer windows. A Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct evaluation shows near-random separability and reverses the preferred windowing behavior, with accumulated scoring becoming strongest.119:T644,The method is simple at its core. In standard policy-gradient estimation, the coefficient multiplying each sample’s score-function term is approximately the product of the importance-sampling ratio r and the advantage A. PPO clips only r within a trust region, but if A is large, the effective coefficient rA can still be large and noisy. ACPO clips this product directly to the interval [-alpha, alpha], thereby controlling the actual scalar that scales each sample’s policy-gradient contribution. This has two immediate consequences: both large positive and large negative advantages are constrained in a unified way, and the clipping target is better aligned with the true update magnitude. The paper also shows that ACPO can be plugged into PPO- and GRPO-style pipelines without redesigning the whole training loop. The theory has two parts. First, under explicit assumptions, the second moment of the ACPO gradient estimator is no larger than that of PPO; with an additional assumption, this yields a variance-reduction guarantee. The point is not a strong optimality theorem, but a formal explanation of why clipping rA should be more stable than clipping r alone. Second, the authors connect ACPO to policy mirror descent by interpreting it as the policy-optimization analogue of gradient clipping, and they derive convergence guarantees for gradient-clipped PMD in standard RL settings. Relative to prior work, the novelty is not in a new critic, reward shaping, or rollout scheme, but in changing the clipping target from the IS ratio to the quantity that actually controls update magnitude.11a:T475,The experiments use Qwen2.5-Math-7B and Qwen3 models at 1.7B, 4B, and 8B scales, evaluated on four mathematical reasoning benchmarks with eight matched comparisons. ACPO improves the best observed weighted accuracy in all eight comparisons: gains are reported as 1.6 to 4.0 points over PPO and 0.6 to 1.5 points over GRPO. In terms of training efficiency, it reaches each baseline’s best observed performance in substantially fewer steps, with reported speedups of about 6.25x over PPO and 1.7x over GRPO. Another notable result is that PPO-AC remains competitive with GRPO while using only one rollout per prompt, which suggests the gain is not merely from more sampling but from better gradient control. When reading the full paper, the most informative evidence is likely in the training curves and variance-related diagnostics rather than the final accuracy alone, because the central claim is about stability and efficiency. If the trend holds across these settings, the method is less likely to be a recipe-specific artifact.11b:T4ab,For a quick but useful read, start with the introduction and the algorithm definition to pin down the exact change: this is not a new large objective framework, but a replacement of ratio clipping with ratio-times-advantage clipping. The goal on first pass is to understand what is being guaranteed and under which assumptions, not to absorb every proof detail. After that, go straight to the main result tables and training curves, and check three things: whether final performance is consistently better, whether the same performance is reached faster, and whether the benefit survives in the one-rollout setting. The deeper questions are whether noisy advantage estimates could suppress genuinely valuable high-advantage samples too early, and whether a fixed clipping threshold alpha remains appropriate in longer-horizon, sparser-reward RL settings.11c:T835,方法上，这篇文章不是发明新的 OPSD 变体，而是围绕标准 OPSD 做了大规模受控拆解。基础设定是：student 按当前策略 on-policy 采样完整推理轨迹；teacher 是 student 初始参数的冻结副本，但在输入端额外看到 privileged context，例如完整参考解或已验证答案；teacher 在 student 访问到的每个 prefix 上给出 next-token 分布，训练目标是让 student 贴近 teacher。默认损失是 clipped forward KL，对每个词表项的 KL 贡献做上限裁剪，以抑制极端 token 的梯度。关键分析点有几个。其一，作者显式区分 student 和 teacher 的推理模式 m_S, m_T∈{Think, No-think}，并把“reasoning-mode mismatch”作为核心变量。实验显示，teacher 信号的变化很大程度来自 teacher 是否处在 think 模式，以及 teacher 是否拿到完整 teacher prefix，而不是 privileged context 的语义本身。换言之，teacher 在不同模式下会诱导完全不同的 token 分布，student 学到的是这种模式化行为。其二，作者对 teacher context 做了细粒度 ablation，比较 full-solution、answer-only、去掉 privileged semantics 但保留 prefix 结构等设置，发现只删语义内容时分布变化并不大，而改变 prefix 构造和模式对齐时影响更显著。其三，作者系统比较不同 KL 方向和配置。虽然原始 OPSD 常用 forward KL，但不同模型上 forward / reverse / clipped 版本的效果并不一致，说明这里不是一个简单的“teacher 更准所以 forward KL 更好”的故事，而是和 teacher 分布尖锐度、student rollout 偏移、训练稳定性共同作用。其四，作者还尝试了 token selection redesign，例如基于 loss 或 entropy 选择更“有信息量”的 token 更新，但没有得到稳定收益。这一点很重要，因为它说明问题不只是无效 token 太多，而是监督信号本身带有系统性偏差。整体上，这篇文章把 OPSD 重新刻画成一种强依赖上下文分布匹配的行为蒸馏，而不是可靠的能力蒸馏。11d:T43f,This is important because it sharpens how self-improvement methods should be interpreted at the pretrain–posttrain boundary. The contribution is diagnostic rather than algorithmic, but it is substantial. First, it reframes OPSD as behavior distillation under shifted conditioning contexts, not reliable capability distillation. Second, it shows that gains live in a narrow regime: model size, rollout length, training duration, teacher context, think/no-think mode pairing, and KL choice all interact, and small changes can turn mild gains into steady degradation or collapse. Third, it identifies which signals are actually useful for monitoring. Initial forward KL is not predictive of the signed downstream effect, while training traces such as length growth, entropy changes, and formatting failures are more informative. For researchers working on RLVR, self-training, or R1-Zero-style bootstrapping, the paper is a useful warning: dense token-level supervision does not automatically mean good credit assignment, especially when teacher and student have almost no capability gap.11e:T739,The paper keeps the standard OPSD setup and performs a careful controlled dissection. The student samples on-policy reasoning trajectories. The teacher is a frozen copy of the student at initialization, but it receives privileged context such as a full reference solution or a verified answer. At every student-visited prefix, the teacher produces a next-token distribution, and the student is trained to match it. The default objective is a clipped forward KL, where each vocabulary contribution is capped to avoid extreme token-level gradients. The key technical contribution is the experimental decomposition. First, the paper explicitly treats student and teacher reasoning modes m_S and m_T in {Think, No-think} as first-class variables. This is crucial: the teacher signal changes strongly with reasoning-mode mismatch, often more than with the semantic content of the privileged context itself. Second, the authors ablate teacher context construction in detail, comparing full-solution context, answer-only context, and variants that remove semantic content while preserving prefix structure. The striking result is that removing semantics alone changes the signal much less than changing the prefix distribution and mode alignment. Third, the paper compares KL variants and finds that the effect of forward versus other divergences is model-dependent. This suggests the issue is not simply that the teacher is better calibrated, but that teacher sharpness, rollout mismatch, and optimization stability interact in nontrivial ways. Fourth, the paper tests token-selection redesigns based on loss or entropy, aiming to focus updates on more informative positions, but these do not provide a consistent fix. The most interesting follow-up questions are whether the same conclusions hold with an EMA self-teacher or a stronger external teacher, whether verifier-style privilege behaves differently from full-solution privilege, and whether the proposed diagnostics can be used as early-stop or curriculum signals in RLVR pipelines.121:T4cb,The proposed procedure is On-Policy Warmup. During warmup, the student interacts with the environment using its own policy. A fixed teacher then provides supervision on the states and histories actually visited by the student, including states reached after bad actions. The student is trained by on-policy distillation. After warmup, teacher queries stop and training switches to RLVR with verifiable outcome rewards. The theoretical analysis treats token or action generation as a finite-horizon trajectory distribution. Under shared environment dynamics, the cumulative reverse-KL distillation loss on student-visited states equals the KL divergence between the student and teacher trajectory distributions. Data processing then bounds the gap between their binary-verifier success probabilities. A competent teacher plus sufficiently small on-policy distillation loss gives a positive lower bound on the student’s initial success probability and an upper bound on the expected number of rollouts needed to discover a success. The paper also analyzes when a higher success probability increases the chance of sampling mixed success/failure groups, which are the groups that provide direct contrast for GRPO-style training.122:T408,The setup follows OPSD. A full-parameter student samples on-policy responses. A frozen teacher, initialized from the same checkpoint, receives the student response plus privileged context and returns next-token distributions. Exact forward KL would sum token-level contributions over the vocabulary and pull the student distribution toward the teacher. The OPSD variant clips each vocabulary-wise contribution at a threshold before summing. The paper analyzes this objective in three steps. First, it derives the logit gradient and shows that gradient descent reverses the correction direction for clipped tokens and for some unclipped tokens whose student probability is above the teacher’s. Second, under fixed clipped and unclipped token sets, it characterizes the minimizer: the objective prefers reducing the total probability of clipped tokens toward zero, while allocating extra probability to the unclipped set. Third, it links this analysis to generation behavior by measuring token probabilities inside repetition loops.123:T431,Neighborhood OPSD builds a pool of frozen local perturbation experts around the original privileged teacher M0. Offline selection scores experts by filtered reference-token gains on reference prefixes: an expert is useful when it raises the probability of the reference token over a problem-only baseline and adds coverage not already provided by the current pool. The greedy selection therefore rewards marginal, non-overlapping corrections rather than overall task accuracy. Online, the student visits its own prefixes, which may differ from the reference solution, so routing cannot use the reference token directly. The selected experts evaluate the student state. MaxPeak chooses the highest-probability token assigned by any expert as the anchor. Quantile selection then chooses among experts whose top token matches that anchor, controlling the level of support so that overly large teacher-student gaps are less likely to be clipped. The chosen expert supplies the full next-token distribution for distillation. Experts stay fixed; deployment uses only the student.124:T455,The paper introduces PersonaUnlearnBench and PaCE. PersonaUnlearnBench builds model-specific paired data: for the same user question, target-persona and desirable-counterpart system instructions are used to elicit paired responses, which are then filtered into aligned forget and retain sets. Held-out questions and paraphrased instructions test whether the edit generalizes beyond construction wording. Evaluation covers target forgetting, counterpart preservation, response quality, and external utility.

PaCE extracts a persona direction from same-question contrasts between target and counterpart responses. It then uses causal probing to choose a layer for editing the pre-generation state. The loss has two parts. An erasure term pushes the target projection below a counterpart-calibrated boundary along the persona direction. An anchor term aligns the orthogonal component with the matched counterpart representation. The design choice matters: simply suppressing target outputs can collapse into refusal or low-quality generation, while the orthogonal anchor keeps a coherent answer route available.125:T4ba,OPSRD uses two contexts for the same base model. The student samples an on-policy reasoning trajectory under an ordinary role-free prompt. A frozen teacher, with the student adapter disabled, receives an expert role prompt and scores the exact same student prefixes. The teacher does not need to generate a complete solution; it supplies next-token distributions at the decision points the student actually visits. Only a low-rank adapter on the student is updated.

The method selects the highest-entropy half of student positions by default, with ρ=0.5, so supervision focuses on uncertain choices rather than syntax or already-determined continuations. Distributions for distillation use temperature η=1.1. Sampling uses top-p=0.95 and top-k=20, while the loss keeps the full vocabulary. The main objective is teacher-weighted forward KL with per-token contribution clipping. The motivation is that reverse KL gives weak correction when the student assigns near-zero probability to alternatives supported by the teacher, whereas forward KL can raise those underestimated alternatives. The paper compares forward KL, reverse KL, Jensen–Shannon divergence, neutral teachers, and different role placements.126:T557,The model samples a rationale and, after an Answer: marker, the method reads the next-token distribution over the K answer options rather than sampling a final answer. Each rationale therefore commits to a distribution u(r). The objective scores that per-rationale distribution using a shifted negated Brier score, with log score behaving similarly in the experiments. The central identity is J(E_r u)=E_r J(u)+Var_r(u) for the Brier score. Scoring the mixture of multiple rationales therefore equals the average per-rationale score plus a disagreement bonus. With one-hot sampled answers, this becomes RLVR plus a Gini-diversity term. Since the bonus does not require grounded disagreement, it can reward randomization. Per-rationale scoring avoids this and has the calibrated optimum u(r)=q(x) for every rationale, so even a single sampled trajectory can return a calibrated probability. The practical recipe is to calibrate first, then reinforce: train the readout distribution first, then reinforce reasoning with the proper score as reward while anchoring the policy with KL to the calibrated model. The analysis identifies two failure modes in end-to-end optimization: System-One collapse, where the model stops using reasoning, and gradient domination, where the policy-gradient term is 7–12 times larger than the readout gradient and overwhelms calibration.127:T4c4,The study uses 751 fine-tuning runs across five Qwen3 models from 0.6B to 32B parameters and Mistral-24B. In two held-out mixture prediction tests, the transfer map has less than half the error of a mixture-agnostic baseline and beats the similarity selector at the tested mixture sizes.128:T773,The authors build PhantomEnvironments by extending PhantomWiki-style fictional worlds into interactive multi-turn RL environments. Each environment consists of templated articles, a randomly sampled relational world structure, and programmatically generated multi-hop questions. The task is not single-shot QA. The model must issue search actions under a budget, inspect retrieved documents, chain evidence across turns, and answer at the end. Rewards are exactly verifiable because the world is generated by rules.

Several design choices matter. First, the pipeline is fully rule-based, so reward computation is clean and benchmark leakage is avoided. Second, environment complexity is explicitly controllable: universe size, question difficulty, and question budget are tunable. The paper further decomposes question distributions into three types—linear hops, attribute comparison, and attribute constraints—which turns the environment into an analysis tool rather than just a data source. Third, the training setup uses full RL fine-tuning of four off-the-shelf instruct models, making the study about whether the environment itself provides a strong enough optimization signal.

Compared with Search-R1-style training on real Wikipedia, the key difference is not merely synthetic versus real text. It is what behavior the environment rewards. Real-world environments mix two gains: better search policy and exploitation of stored factual knowledge. PhantomEnvironments intentionally remove the second route, concentrating learning pressure on search behavior. The ablations also show that complexity dimensions do not compose automatically. Linear-hop questions drive most of the transfer. Comparison questions help specifically on real comparison tasks. Constraint questions can backfire because rare attributes enable one-shot verbatim retrieval, letting the model bypass decomposition entirely.129:T6a7,The study trains four models with RL in PhantomEnvironments: Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, and Phi-4-mini-instruct. Evaluation covers six real-world multi-hop search benchmarks: HotpotQA, 2WikiMultihopQA, MuSiQue, SynthWorlds-RM, SynthWorlds-SM, and FRAMES.

The headline result is strong transfer from fictional environments to real benchmarks. Relative to the base models, RL-trained agents improve by about 1.7x on the Wikipedia-2018-based benchmarks and about 2.2x on the newer, harder benchmarks. The paper also compares PhantomEnvironments directly against Search-R1-style training in a real Wikipedia environment. The real environment wins on in-domain Wikipedia-2018 evaluation, which is expected because memorized knowledge helps there. But that advantage narrows on benchmarks built from newer Wikipedia snapshots, and for Qwen models it disappears. The cleanest evidence comes from the SynthWorlds real-vs-synthetic mirror pair: training on real-world data preserves or widens the RM/SM gap, while training in PhantomEnvironments closes it, consistent with less reliance on snapshot-specific memorization.

The ablations are especially informative. Linear-hop questions account for most of the transfer. Comparison questions improve performance on corresponding real-world comparison tasks. Constraint questions hurt transfer because they reward a shortcut: retrieving the gold document with a single precise query instead of decomposing the problem. Another notable finding is that trained Qwen agents allocate search budget roughly linearly with question difficulty, suggesting an emergent compute-allocation behavior rather than just a static score gain.12a:T7ec,The method centers on building long-horizon reflective trajectories. A task environment is formalized as e=(sigma, S), where sigma is the task specification and S is an executable scoring function. The agent works in the same environment for multiple rounds. In each round it proposes a candidate solution y_t, receives feedback f_t, and decides how to revise the solution next.

The data pipeline has three stages. First, a teacher model converts raw source material from GitHub and online judges into executable environments. In machine learning engineering, these environments include training pipelines, validation metrics, and task constraints. In algorithmic programming, they include problem statements, tests, and judging logic. Second, an agent interacts with each environment over many rounds, generating revision trajectories. Third, trajectories are selected as whole sequences rather than filtered step by step. A trajectory is kept if its final score is high and the process satisfies task requirements, even if intermediate rounds contain failures, regressions, or dead ends. This is the key design choice in the paper, because it preserves the behavioral signal of recovering from setbacks and continuing to improve.

AREX-2 is trained from Qwen3.8-27B on these long-horizon trajectories together with the deep-research data used in the earlier AREX recipe. The underlying hypothesis is that reflection and long-horizon execution are meta-skills. Therefore, the best training domains are not necessarily those that look most similar to the target domain, but those that provide clean supervision, verifiable feedback, and room for sustained improvement.

Compared with common agent-training pipelines, the differences are clear: the target behavior is multi-round improvement rather than one-shot success; the filtering unit is the full trajectory rather than individual successful steps; and domain choice is driven by supervision quality and verifiability rather than surface similarity to the downstream task.12b:T54e,The empirical section is the main strength of the paper. Starting from Qwen3.8-27B, AREX-2 reaches 81.8 on MLE-bench Lite and 70.7 on Frontier-CS, with the latter reported as the best among the open-weight models compared in the paper. More importantly, the gains transfer beyond the training domains. Without adding new deep-research-specific training data, AREX-2 achieves 84.0 on BrowseComp, 52.6 on HLE, 92.2 on GAIA, and 93.8 on DeepSearchQA. That supports the claim that long-horizon reflection learned in verifiable environments can generalize to more open-ended research tasks.

Two experimental patterns matter. First, performance continues to improve as the round budget increases, which suggests the model has learned to convert extra test-time budget into better solutions instead of stalling early. Second, the model is only 27B, yet compares favorably with substantially larger systems, implying that the gain is tied to the training recipe and data rather than scale alone.

FoldingCorpus is built from 1,200 proteins from the OpenFold monomer short-protein collection, split into 1,000 train, 100 dev, and 100 frozen-test proteins with cluster-disjoint partitions. Each forget unit pairs the same question under a deception-triggering context c+ and a neutral context c-, using the model’s own responses. A tuple is kept only when the model’s behavior flips while its apparent belief is preserved, so the dataset records realized deceptions without human annotation. The paper then analyzes why existing unlearning objectives are incomplete. Suppression objectives such as NPO reduce the likelihood of the deceptive continuation but do not specify where probability mass should go, so the model may produce other bad continuations. Target-based objectives, such as counterfactual distillation, copy the neutral-context behavior into the pressured context, with a fixed point close to πθ(·|x,c+) = π0(·|x,c-). They remove deception well, but cause context blindness: the model behaves as if the system prompt or user pressure were absent, losing benign instruction following, secret-keeping, and explicit recognition of the pressure in its reasoning. Pact addresses this by using targets that keep the honest answer and reasoning while explicitly acknowledging the pressure or instruction and stating that it should not change the answer. An attack-aware term is added to improve resistance to short re-finetuning attacks.12f:T759,The method starts from self-distillation, but the key idea is to make it position-selective. A student judge generates a trace and final verdict from input (x, yA, yB). A teacher, instantiated from the same base model but additionally conditioned on natural-language feedback, provides next-token distributions along the student's rollout. This already differs from outcome-supervised RL because criterion-choice tokens now receive direct local supervision shaped by the rationale.

The main technical contribution is the entropy-shift analysis. For each position, the paper measures the change in entropy between the teacher and student next-token distributions after conditioning the teacher on feedback. This yields two regimes. In context sharpening, entropy drops sharply and the teacher concentrates probability on a narrow expression aligned with the feedback. In context spreading, entropy increases or lies in the lower tail of the per-sequence entropy-shift distribution, meaning the teacher preserves multiple feedback-consistent alternatives. The paper interprets sharpening as encouraging memorization of a particular phrasing, while spreading better preserves semantic understanding of the criterion.

Based on this, the authors propose masking positions for distillation using entropy shift. They keep the lower tail of the entropy-shift distribution within each generation and remove the highest-shift positions from the distillation loss. So the student is not forced to imitate every confident teacher token. Instead, it is trained more on positions where feedback constrains meaning without collapsing to one fixed wording. Relative to naive self-distillation, the difference is exactly this selective filtering. Relative to outcome-supervised RL, the difference is dense token-level supervision informed by language feedback rather than a single verdict reward.130:T5f9,The empirical story has three parts. First, self-distilled judges outperform outcome-supervised RL on subjective evaluation categories, with reported gains of 2 to 9 percentage points over Dr. GRPO. Second, Dr. GRPO remains competitive on objective subcategories, which supports the paper's framing that RL is better matched to application rigor when the criterion is clear-cut. Third, adding entropy-shift masking improves OOD generalization over naive self-distillation, suggesting the gain comes from better supervision placement rather than simply more supervision.

The paper reports training curves on RM-Bench for Qwen3-4B-Instruct and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct. SD+mask consistently leads both naive SD and Dr. GRPO during training. Two deeper questions are worth keeping in mind while reading. First, how robust is entropy shift as a selection signal if the teacher is miscalibrated? Second, can this framework extend beyond judge training to process supervision or explanation-conditioned language modeling more broadly? A quick read takes about 20 to 30 minutes. A careful read with figures and ablations is closer to an hour.132:T715,The method, GRGC, has two coupled components. The first is critic-side geometry calibration. The authors note that a critic trained only for teacher-student discrimination can assign student rewards that are all packed together, making within-group ranking fragile under noise. To fix this, they add a Gaussian groupwise Optimal Transport calibration term during critic training. For each prompt, the sorted student rewards are aligned to group-centered Gaussian quantiles. The goal is not to force rewards to be Gaussian per se, but to induce a non-degenerate spread, smoother rank gaps, and a more stable scale. The choice of Gaussian quantiles is motivated by their symmetric and moderate spacing profile, which gives a controlled margin structure without the harshness of hard-margin constraints or ad hoc binning.

The second component is policy-side group modulation. After critic-side calibration, each reward group is centered and normalized, then passed through a signed power transform. This amplifies informative within-group differences while preserving ordering. The point is not to redefine the reward semantics, but to make the resulting advantages more separable and more robust for GRPO updates. The paper also provides propositions connecting this geometry to optimization: under a grouped softmax surrogate, advantage gaps directly determine one-step pairwise log-odds shifts; under clipped GRPO, advantage errors induce bounded distortion in the surrogate objective. So reward geometry is treated as a first-order optimization variable, not a cosmetic property.

Relative to prior work such as GAD, the novelty is not a stronger critic architecture or more teacher queries. The novelty is to explicitly condition the critic outputs so that they are well-formed for grouped policy optimization.133:T60f,From the provided full text, the experimental setup spans multiple teachers, multiple student families and scales, and multiple training datasets. The evaluation covers both in-distribution and out-of-distribution benchmarks, and uses different auto-judges, metrics, and human preference evaluation to test robustness. The central empirical claim is that GRGC consistently improves over existing on-policy adversarial black-box distillation baselines and over simpler SeqKD-style approaches.

However, the supplied text does not include the full result tables, exact model sizes, training-token counts, group size settings, or precise gains on each benchmark. So it would be unsafe to invent concrete numbers. What can be stated with confidence is the structure of the evidence:
1. Main results: gains hold across teacher choices, student architectures, and datasets.
2. Mechanistic validation: the paper measures reward-group dispersion, scale, ranking stability, and downstream advantage separability, linking performance gains to improved reward geometry rather than incidental tuning.
3. Robustness checks: conclusions remain under different judges, metrics, and human preference evaluation, which reduces the chance that the method is merely overfitting to one evaluator.

If the full paper is available later, the most important numbers to extract are the average gain over GAD, sensitivity to group size, ablations for OT calibration and signed power modulation separately, and intermediate statistics such as reward variance or rank-flip rate.134:T86b,方法建立在 Sparta Alignment 式的多模型协同框架上，但把 instruction sampling 提升为 leader-follower 的 Stackelberg game。leader 不是生成答案的模型，而是一个控制 instruction 分布的 bandit；followers 才是参与 duel 并通过偏好信号更新的 LLM 池。每轮训练中，leader 从 instruction pool 上给出采样分布，随后进行 D 次 duel。每次 duel 选一条 instruction，两名模型作答，其余模型做 peer judges，在给定分数区间内对回答打分，再聚合成 preference pairs 用于 RL fine-tuning。

核心创新在 leader 的更新规则。作者使用 EXP3，而不是 UCB 或简单 moving-average reweighting，原因是 reward 非平稳：同一条 instruction 的价值会随着模型能力变化而改变，而且不同 instruction 的反馈噪声较大。EXP3 适合 adversarial / non-stationary bandit 场景，并且天然支持只观察被采样臂的 bandit feedback。为了避免 leader 只追逐“难题”或只追逐“分歧大但无意义的题”，论文设计了 composite reward，把 instruction difficulty 与 duel discriminability 结合起来。前者刻画题目是否仍具挑战性，后者刻画该题是否能稳定地产生可学习的胜负差异。只有同时具备一定难度、又能区分模型优劣的 instruction，才会被持续加权。

另一个关键部件是 reputation 机制。每个模型维护历史 duel 表现得到的 reputation，未参赛模型作为 judge 时，其投票按 reputation 加权；参赛对手的匹配也按 reputation 接近原则进行，避免强弱差距过大导致 duel 失去信息量。这一点延续了 Sparta 的思想，但在这里与 adaptive instruction selection 形成耦合：题目和对手都被调到“刚好能产生学习信号”的区域。方法上值得注意的设计细节还有两点。其一，每轮并不遍历整个 instruction pool，而是只按 leader 分布抽样固定预算的 duel，这不是近似实现，而是课程学习本身。其二，采样分布保留非零 floor probability，避免某些 instruction 被永久遗忘，从而保留探索能力。135:T894,The framework is cast as a Stackelberg game. A leader chooses a distribution over the instruction pool, and the follower models then duel on sampled instructions and update from the resulting preference data. Concretely, at each training iteration the leader defines a sampling distribution over instructions, and D duels are drawn from that distribution with replacement. In each duel, two models answer the selected instruction, while the remaining models act as peer judges and score the responses. These scores are aggregated into preference pairs for RL fine-tuning.

The central technical choice is to implement the leader with EXP3 rather than a simpler heuristic or a stationary bandit. That choice is motivated by non-stationary rewards: the usefulness of an instruction changes as the model pool improves, and only sampled instructions reveal feedback. The reward is composite, combining instruction difficulty with duel discriminability. This is important. Difficulty alone would overemphasize questions that are too hard to learn from; discriminability alone would overemphasize shallow questions that separate models but no longer push the frontier. The leader therefore shifts probability mass toward instructions that are both challenging and still capable of producing informative preference signal.

A second component is the reputation mechanism inherited and extended from prior collaborative alignment work. Each model maintains a reputation score based on past duel outcomes. When a model serves as a judge, its vote is weighted by reputation. When duel participants are selected, models are matched by reputation proximity so that contests remain competitive. This interacts naturally with adaptive instruction selection: both the task and the opponent are kept near the current learning frontier. Two implementation details are also worth noting. First, the method intentionally does not sweep the full instruction pool every iteration; sparse sampling under a fixed duel budget is the curriculum mechanism, not an approximation artifact. Second, the leader keeps a nonzero probability floor for every instruction, preserving exploration and preventing permanent exclusion.136:T6df,The evaluation uses three heterogeneous model pools—specialized expert models, academic research models, and general-purpose models—across 12 benchmarks spanning scientific discovery, reasoning, coding, instruction following, and knowledge tasks. The main result is consistent: Stackelberg Alignment achieves the best macro-average in all three pools. The reported gains reach up to 7.4% over other training-time collaborative algorithms and 12–25% over the best static inference-time baseline.

The more informative part is the ablation evidence. The paper shows that the gains are not merely from adding another control module, but from adaptive curriculum itself. Replacing the learned leader with uniform instruction sampling leads to systematic degradation. Using only difficulty or only discriminability in the reward is also weaker than the composite reward, which supports the paper’s claim that informative instructions must be both learnable and differentiating. Reputation-weighted judging and reputation-based opponent matching contribute additional stability by reducing noisy preference labels and trivial mismatches. The paper also analyzes how the instruction distribution moves during training: earlier iterations focus more on medium-difficulty, high-disagreement instructions, while later iterations shift toward previously too-hard instructions that become learnable as the pool improves. That trajectory is consistent with the proposed moving-disagreement-frontier hypothesis.

For reading the results, the right unit of comparison is duel budget rather than epochs over the instruction set. The method is explicitly budgeted by sampled duels per iteration, so sample efficiency should be interpreted under equal interaction cost.137:T431,Start with the introduction and Figure 1 to understand the actual question: not how models judge each other, but how the system decides which instructions are worth spending duel budget on today.
