Multiple Planning Writers independently search and read sources, then propose candidate structures. A Planning Judge consolidates them, a Critic looks for missing questions and cases, and a Reviser folds the feedback back into the specification. ResearchSpec stores each section’s scope, research questions, required entities or cases, provisional source leads, and hierarchical section IDs. Validators check ID uniqueness, parent-child consistency, consecutive ordering, and required fields before dispatch. Each Researcher then receives the full ResearchSpec plus one section assignment, conducts further evidence gathering in an independent context, and writes a complete section. The assembled draft is reviewed by a Global Editor, while Local Editors apply targeted revisions to affected sections. The design trades some flexibility for controllability: the plan is refined before dispatch and then held fixed during section research.190:T6bf,The system has three parts. The first is a persistent context graph. Instead of storing history as a flat sequence of messages, the system keeps messages, tool calls, and full tool results as persistent nodes, preserving chronology and references. This matters because omitted results are not destroyed; they remain recoverable later.

The second is Tool-Flow Analysis (TFA), which is the main technical idea. TFA tracks how values introduced by earlier tool results are reused in later model steps and tool calls. When a later operation uses a value that originated in an earlier result, the system records an execution dependency and treats it as observed reuse. This is different from standard retrieval memory: the signal is not only whether an old chunk looks relevant to the current query, but whether the execution trace has already shown that the old result supports later actions.

The third is the renderer. Before each model invocation, it selects which historical tool results to expose within a fixed token budget. Selection combines three signals: observed reuse, recency, and semantic relevance. Unselected results stay in the graph and can be restored later. This is a more conservative design than aggressive summarization, because summaries often discard details whose importance only becomes clear much later.

A notable design choice is that the paper does not rely on a learned memory controller or model-driven compression policy. It uses explicit structured state plus hand-designed signals. The upside is interpretability and recoverability. The limitation is that TFA will only be as good as its ability to detect value flow; abstract semantic reuse is likely harder than literal or near-literal reuse.191:T4e1,The evaluation uses two benchmarks, AppWorld and 8-objective QA, with three execution models. The main setting allocates a 6K history budget for prior execution steps rather than passing the full accumulated history. Under this budget, ContextRender reaches task performance close to, and sometimes above, full-history prompting while reducing mean standardized inference cost by 10.2% to 32.2% relative to full history.

Against managed-context baselines, it delivers the best overall task performance across both benchmarks and all three models in the primary setting. The main point is not a single benchmark number, but the fact that it remains competitive under a much smaller visible history budget while preserving recoverability of omitted full results.

The ablations are the most informative part. Adding observed reuse on top of recency and semantic relevance improves both task performance and recall of results that are reused later. The gains are especially large for results reused after long gaps. That directly supports the paper’s claim: long-range execution dependencies are poorly handled by recency-only heuristics, and semantic relevance alone can undervalue tool outputs dominated by identifiers, paths, or parameter values.192:T4b9,The paper contributes a measurement framework and a clean counterfactual design. First, it operationalizes factionalism through interaction traces. In each round, every agent makes an observable commitment and sends that commitment plus a short message to selected peers. From this trace, the authors build a directed weighted agreement graph. An edge from agent i to agent j gains weight when j's next-round commitment matches the commitment that i sent to j. The normalization is important: it controls for contact frequency and convergence timing, so the metric reflects alignment conditional on communication rather than raw message volume.

Second, the experimental design isolates label effects from model effects. The same underlying agents and tasks are run under different visible-label conditions: true family labels, shuffled family labels, neutral labels such as colors, and no visible identity. This is the core methodological move. It separates clustering caused by actual model differences from clustering caused by the mere presence of a label. The reported outcome is that the grouping follows the visible label, including shuffled and neutral labels, rather than the underlying model family.193:T543,FlowMAS models workflow construction as trajectory generation with a GFlowNet. A state corresponds to a partially built workflow topology, actions extend the topology, and a terminal state is a complete workflow. The GFlowNet is trained so that terminal workflows are sampled in proportion to their rewards, which encourages a distribution over high-reward candidates rather than a single optimized graph.

The paper adds two components on top of a vanilla GFlowNet. The information-guided module uses Partial Information Decomposition to estimate how different operators contribute unique, redundant, and synergistic information toward the task. This gives more structured credit assignment than a single scalar textual critique. The curiosity-driven module rewards structural novelty, pushing the generator to explore underrepresented workflow patterns and reducing collapse to a few templates.

Compared with search-based systems such as ADAS and AFlow, FlowMAS learns a reusable topology generator instead of repeatedly searching a large tree. Compared with textual-gradient methods such as OneFlow and DebFlow, it aims for finer-grained structural feedback. Compared with VAE, graph diffusion, or MLP-based generators, the paper argues that GFlowNets are a better fit for discrete graph-like objects with reward-driven diversity requirements.194:T5a8,Core represents a reasoning trajectory as a stack of decisions. Each decision has a stable identifier, dependencies, and a canonical key that preserves type, value, dependency context, and occurrence identity when needed. A proposer, which may be an LLM or a deterministic policy, returns a finite ordered list of candidates for the next decision. The verifier returns pass, fail(C), or unknown. A fail(C) output is only eligible for hard caching when C is a sound conflict core: no valid complete solution can contain all decision keys in C. The controller keeps a stack and a set of learned nogoods. Before verifying a candidate, it checks whether the resulting state contains a cached core; if so, the candidate is skipped without another verifier call. When a certified failure is found, Core optionally minimizes the core, inserts it into the cache, removes stored supersets, and backjumps to the latest decision contained in the core. Later decisions are discarded because they cannot repair a conflict that does not mention them. If all candidates at a level are exhausted, their explanations can be resolved into an exhaustion core. Unknown verifier outputs can extend the stack provisionally, but they cannot create hard constraints. The formal guarantees require sound verification, sound cores, finite branching and depth, and exhaustive proposals; under these assumptions, uncapped search is complete and does not prune valid solutions.195:T5b8,The paper audits a Dr. Zero-style proposer-solver loop after training. For each scheduled step, it saves the source document, the adopted pseudo-label, and the five solver responses used to compute proposer reward. An independent evidence-based auditor builds a reference from the source and judges the saved labels and responses; unsupported cases are left unresolved rather than forced into a binary label. The metrics separate several effects: T_P is pseudo-label correctness, T_S is solver-response correctness, A is the in-loop match rate, F is false-agreement mass where the label and solver response match but are both wrong, and L counts correct solver answers denied credit by a wrong label. Two mitigations are tested. Multi-sample verification samples the same model three times with the source and three times without the source, admitting a proposal only when the majorities are compatible. This improves label quality but adds six generations per candidate and does not fully remove the failure. CrossFit is the main intervention. Source documents are split into two groups. One auxiliary solver trains only on group A and scores questions generated from group B; the other trains only on group B and scores questions from group A. These cross-fitted scores shape proposer reward, while the main solver still trains on all admitted questions. This blocks the direct path where a solver is rewarded for repeating an error learned from the same source.196:T551,The method is simple, but the experimental control is strong. Mid-Harness keeps the generator, execution harness, and serving setup unchanged. It only inserts an intermediate wrapper: given the same interaction history, sample several candidate actions, apply a verifier, and forward only the selected action to the original harness. This makes it possible to separate two questions: whether the generator already contains useful alternatives, and whether a verifier can identify them before execution. The paper varies candidate width, verification mechanism, and verifier capability. A key setting is self-verification, where the same model both generates and verifies. In that regime, wider sampling helps little, which indicates that the bottleneck is discrimination rather than candidate diversity. The paper compares pointwise and pairwise verification and finds pairwise comparison works best, likely because candidate actions differ in intent, semantics, and environmental fit in ways that are easier to judge relatively than absolutely. The authors then distill a verifier initialized from the generator using pairwise judgments from GPT-5.6 Sol, while leaving the action generator unchanged. This is a useful design because it separates the upper bound enabled by a strong verifier from the portion that can be recovered by a practical local verifier.197:T555,The main experiments use a fixed TMAX-9B generator on TerminalBench-Lite. There are three key findings. First, with a strong verifier, GPT-5.6 Sol raises Pass@1 from 50.00% for the base agent to 68.03%, showing that the generator already produces many useful alternatives that the default pipeline fails to select reliably. Second, under self-verification, increasing candidate width yields only marginal gains, and pairwise verification is the best among the tested mechanisms. Third, distilling a verifier from GPT-5.6 Sol pairwise responses improves Pass@1 from 54.76% to 57.14% without changing the generator. The gain is smaller than using the frontier verifier directly, but it confirms that part of the opportunity can be recovered through verifier training alone. The disagreement analysis is also informative: the main remaining gaps are command semantics and execution feasibility, meaning the verifier still struggles to predict what a command will actually do and whether it will work in the current environment. The paper also shows compatibility with trajectory-level scaling. Mid-Harness improves both parallel scaling with Best-of-T trajectories and sequential scaling with Sequential Refine. In particular, TMAX-9B plus one round of Sequential Refine and Mid-Harness outperforms Best-of-T at T=7 while using less than half the estimated token cost.198:T720,The method is called Retrospective World Modeling (RWM). Instead of relying only on a forward model of the form P(s_{t+1} | s_t, a_t), the agent is also trained to reason backward and infer the action responsible for an observed transition, conceptually P(â_t | s_t, s_{t+1}). Importantly, this is not presented as a standalone inverse-dynamics model bolted onto the side. The retrospective capability is integrated into the unified policy network and used directly for policy optimization.

On top of this, the paper introduces Self-Consistency Reward (SCR). The intuition is simple: if the action chosen by the policy is also the action that the retrospective model would infer from the resulting transition, then the action is more causally grounded and should receive higher intrinsic reward. If the two disagree, the policy is acting in a way that is poorly explained by the actual environment dynamics. This turns the usual observe-predict-act loop into a closed loop with retrospective verification. The authors explicitly distinguish SCR from curiosity-style bonuses. Curiosity rewards novelty or prediction error and tends to encourage exploration; SCR is designed as an exploitation-oriented regularizer that favors actions whose consequences can be consistently explained after the fact.

A technically important part of the paper is its treatment of reward hacking. Retrospective consistency can be gamed if the model exploits superficial transition cues or if the retrospective module is given too much contextual information. The paper therefore studies different reward formulations and context regulation strategies to prevent leakage and shortcut solutions. That section is central to judging whether the method is learning causal grounding or merely benefiting from an overly informative auxiliary signal.199:T652,The paper evaluates the method on multiple agentic tasks and reports a headline improvement in average success rate from 8% to 81%, together with stronger generalization. Because the gain is large, the experimental setup matters a lot: readers should check task difficulty, action space, observability, and whether training budgets are matched. From the full text, the intended comparison is not only against plain RL agents but also against agents equipped with prospective world modeling, so the claimed benefit is specifically from retrospective verification rather than from adding another auxiliary head.

Two experimental messages stand out. First, RWM with SCR improves convergence speed and action effectiveness in long-horizon settings, suggesting that retrospective consistency provides denser credit assignment than sparse task rewards alone. Second, the ablations indicate that this signal needs to be internalized into policy optimization; using retrospective reasoning only as an analysis tool or side objective is weaker. The paper also compares alternative reward formulations and context regulation strategies, explicitly measuring the impact of reward hacking mitigation.

Given the aggressive headline number, the most useful reading strategy is to verify where that 8%→81% jump comes from: whether it is averaged over all tasks, concentrated on a subset of hard environments, or dependent on specific partial-observability settings. If the setup is sound, the main takeaway is that retrospective consistency can materially improve long-horizon RL training, not just next-state prediction quality.19a:T408,Start with the introduction and Figure 1 to understand the conceptual distinction between prospective and retrospective world modeling. Then go straight to the definition of SCR in the method section. The exact form matters: whether it is based on action matching probability, log-probability, margin, or another consistency score determines whether the method behaves more like reward shaping, an auxiliary objective, or an implicit verifier.

In the experiments, prioritize three parts: the main results table to see where the gains occur, the ablations removing the retrospective module or SCR, and the analysis of reward formulations and context regulation. Those sections tell you whether the method is robust or just exploiting a favorable setup. For a skim-level read, 25–35 minutes is enough. If reading more deeply, a useful follow-up question is whether the same idea could transfer to LLM tool-use trajectories, where one could score actions by whether the resulting state change makes them retrospectively explainable.19b:T85b,The paper formulates recursive social improvement as an RL problem over a population of N agents. Agent i faces its own task distribution D_i and is rewarded only on its own tasks. Each round has two decisions. First, the agent chooses a learning action: search privately, observe a peer, or abstain. Second, it chooses a task action by executing a skill from its current library. A skill can be a simple option in a controlled environment or a full skill file in the LLM setting.

A central design choice is token accounting. Search, observation, and acting all draw from the same budget, and the cost of discovering a copied skill is counted as part of the total social-learning cost. This avoids the common mistake of treating copied knowledge as free.

The experiments proceed in two stages. In the controlled stage, options have known value structure, allowing the authors to test whether established social-learning algorithms can in principle yield an advantage. In the LLM stage, agents write, revise, and exchange skill files for instruction-following tasks. These skill files are inference-time textual procedures rather than weight updates. Policies are implemented by fixed-weight LLMs learning in context: the model decides whether to revise its own skill, copy a peer’s skill, or act.

The paper also makes an important distinction between two notions of success. Efficient social learning means better performance per token. Effective social learning means higher final performance than independent learners at the same total cost. This distinction is one of the strongest parts of the paper because many multi-agent results show speed or cost gains without showing superiority under matched compute.

The authors further test simple interventions such as reserving tokens for acting and requiring some private search. These do not resolve the core issue. Another notable analysis tracks skill lineage over time. Copied skills are often revised again, so the process is not mere imitation. But most final skills end up tracing back to only one or two early revisions, indicating rapid lineage collapse and path dependence.19c:T6d7,The empirical picture is consistent and informative. In the controlled environment, a hand-designed social-learning policy does achieve a social advantage. That shows the setting itself does not rule out social learning. The failure appears when LLMs are used as the policy controllers.

Across tested LLMs, populations with peer observation are 30% to 52% less efficient than solo populations of the same model. In other words, useful social information exists, but the models do not manage it well enough; they reduce exploration too aggressively.

In the skill-file experiments, peer access changes learning speed and cost but not the matched-cost conclusion. With peer access, GLM-5.3-Flash achieves on average 1.3 percentage points higher held-out accuracy over the course of learning. GPT-OSS-120B uses about one-third fewer learning tokens. These are real benefits, but they are benefits in trajectory shape or efficiency, not in final performance at equal token cost. When learning tokens are matched, neither model shows a clear advantage over independent learners.

The lineage analysis is especially useful. Skills are copied and then revised again, so there is genuine recursive improvement. But by the end, most agents’ skills descend from only one or two of the population’s earliest revisions. This explains the main negative result: copied options often beat what an agent found alone at that moment, yet population-level exploration collapses, so the group does not surpass independent search overall.

The paper is careful not to oversell a benchmark win. Its strongest evidence comes from matched-token comparisons that separate “social learning looks smarter” from “social learning is actually better under equal cost.”19d:T4bf,A good reading order is: formal problem setup, controlled environment results, LLM skill-file experiments, then lineage analysis. About 30–45 minutes is enough for a solid skim.

Pay attention to four parts. First, the RL formulation, especially the two-stage action space and the token accounting. That is what makes the comparisons meaningful. Second, the distinction between efficient and effective social learning. It is the paper’s cleanest conceptual contribution. Third, the contrast between the controlled environment and the LLM setting, because it localizes the failure to the policy controller rather than to the availability of social information. Fourth, any lineage or ancestry figures, since they explain why populations collapse onto a few early discoveries.

If you work on self-improvement, agent training, or inference-time optimization, the natural follow-up question is whether explicit RL, population-based training, or better incentives could learn a stronger copy-versus-search policy than a generic in-context LLM policy. Another useful angle is the connection between transferable skill files and post-training practices such as trajectory reuse, distillation, and synthetic curricula.19e:T445,SkillSeek is a deterministic two-stage retriever exposed as an MCP server, so it can be used by harnesses such as Claude Code, Codex CLI, and OpenHands without changing the agent implementation. Stage 1 uses a BGE-base bi-encoder with 110M parameters and 768-dimensional embeddings to score all indexed skills by cosine similarity and retrieve the top 20. Stage 2 uses a bge-reranker-v2-m3 cross-encoder with 568M parameters to jointly score each query-skill pair and return the top 5. The indexed text is not the full SKILL.md body. It is the skill name and description plus a Tool-REX v3 structured profile containing four tags: file type, primary operation, and two secondary operations. This is a practical design choice: name and description alone often miss the surface forms needed by the reranker, while appending the full body adds noise. The Tool-REX tags are generated offline by an LLM, and online retrieval uses no LLM tokens. The analysis also swaps the stage-2 reranker for Qwen3-Reranker variants and commercial rerankers while keeping the bi-encoder and indexing format fixed.19f:T40a,The evaluation uses the 89-task SkillsBench benchmark over a 4-by-11 grid of pool, backbone, and retrieval method settings. Several numbers are useful. Loading all skills into context is not effective: even with a small 192-skill pool, pass rate stays around the no-skill baseline while token cost rises by 59%. Adding more retrieved skills is also non-monotonic: one relevant skill gives a +17.8% pass-rate lift, two to three skills give +18.6%, and four or more drop to +5.9%. In the headline 34K-skill pool with Qwen3.5-397B-A17B, the SkillSeek variant using Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B reaches a 0.442 pass rate, matching Liu et al. (2026b)’s liu_refined loop. SkillSeek runs on CPU, uses zero online LLM tokens, and keeps cost near the no-skill floor at $27.54.1a0:T47b,The paper models memory use as U(q, M), the observable behavior of a system given query q and memory state M. The observation may include retrieved memories, ranking, or the final memory-dependent response. It then separates failures into two groups. Query-related failures keep M fixed and change q, such as paraphrases that should retrieve the same memory or unsupported queries that should not retrieve unrelated records. Memory-state failures keep q fixed and change M, such as stale records outranking updated records, conflicts being handled incorrectly, or deleted memories still being retrieved. U-Fuzz starts from memory checkpoints produced by normal interactions, builds test seeds from associated queries, and mutates one input dimension at a time. Query mutations preserve meaning, redirect to another supported target, or turn the request into an unsupported one. State mutations update, delete, or modify unrelated memories. Each mutant is validated before execution, and mutation obligations ensure systematic coverage of applicable operator-target pairs. Search is guided by observed memory behavior, not by hidden failure labels.1a1:T42b,SAGE has three components. First, it builds self-explored priors by traversing interactive elements on real devices, constructing a deduplicated UI transition graph, and using a multimodal annotator to synthesize task-trajectory pairs from reachable paths. Second, it creates drift-aware perturbations. The drift taxonomy comes from comparing old and new app versions and includes step insertion or deletion, entry-point and path shifts, control renaming, goal-mismatched detours, and distracting alternatives. Perturbation operators transform clean priors into a distribution that approximates deployment-time retrieval noise, with deterministic reliability labels. Third, it trains a reliability-gated policy. The policy first predicts a reliability variable r in {Follow, Partial, Ignore}, then generates the action conditioned on that decision: p(a|·)=Σr p(r|·)p(a|·,r). This factorization makes the agent explicitly check whether the retrieved path matches the current goal and state before acting, rather than blindly conditioning on retrieved trajectories.1a2:T70a,The paper analyzes discrete heavy-ball momentum dynamics in a river-valley model of the loss landscape. The geometry is decomposed into a low-loss, low-curvature, slowly bending river manifold and sharp orthogonal valley directions. The optimization challenge is not merely to descend, but to move quickly along the river without letting oscillations in the sharp directions destabilize the trajectory.

The main result is that momentum enlarges the largest tolerable learning rate by a leading factor of roughly (1+β)/(1-β) relative to vanilla GD. This factor is classical for quadratic objectives, but the nontrivial part here is showing that it still governs the leading stability threshold in a non-convex setting where the river and valley subspaces rotate and interact over time. Because of that rotation, gradient and momentum components leak across subspaces, so one cannot reuse a fixed-eigenspace argument.

To handle this, the authors develop a new inductive analysis that tracks both gradient and momentum projections onto river and valley directions, while controlling their mutual interference across iterations. A second key conclusion is interpretive: for a flat and slowly spinning river, momentum itself does not substantially change the intrinsic speed along the river. The acceleration mainly comes from enabling a much larger stable learning rate. In that sense, momentum acts more as a stabilizer that permits aggressive step sizes than as a direct source of extra river-direction acceleration.

The paper also improves the largest tolerable learning-rate bound for vanilla GD in the same river-valley framework. That side result suggests the proof machinery is not narrowly tailored to momentum alone, but strengthens the analytical understanding of the landscape model itself.1a3:T5fb,From the available full-text content, this is primarily a theory paper, with experiments serving to validate the mechanism rather than to establish a new large-scale training recipe. The empirical phenomenon tied to the theory is clear: under WSD-like schedules, a long high-LR phase can produce higher observed loss than cosine scheduling because of oscillations across sharp valley walls, while still making faster progress along the river. Once the learning rate is sharply decayed, those oscillations are suppressed and the hidden progress becomes visible as a lower final loss.

The paper also mentions synthetic river-valley loss constructions for visualization and connects its analysis to prior probing of LLM pretraining landscapes in Wen et al. (2025). The most important empirical checks are therefore: (1) momentum remains stable at larger learning rates on synthetic river-valley landscapes; (2) the predicted stability-threshold enlargement matches the observed stable region; and (3) the seemingly paradoxical pattern of higher intermediate loss but better final optimization can be explained by separating river progress from valley oscillation.

The provided text does not include full tables, model sizes, dataset sizes, or exact improvement numbers, so those should not be invented. When reading the original, the most useful experimental artifacts to extract are the stability-boundary plots, the comparisons against vanilla GD, and any quantitative alignment between the theorem and observed training dynamics.1a4:T58c,Read it in the order of phenomenon, model, theorem, then proof technique.

Start with the introduction and lock onto the practical question: why can a long high-LR phase plus sharp decay outperform smoother schedules, and what role does momentum play there? Then jump to Theorem 4.1. That is the central statement of the paper: the maximum stable learning rate is enlarged by about (1+β)/(1-β).

After that, spend time on Lemma 5.1 and the surrounding proof structure. This is where the real novelty sits. The important part is not only the final factor, but how the authors control dynamics when the river and valley subspaces rotate and when gradient and momentum components interfere with each other. While reading, focus on three things: how the river/valley projections are defined and updated, what assumptions encode “flat” and “slow-spinning,” and how the error terms are prevented from accumulating into instability.

If time is limited, read the theorem statements, proof sketches, and the main figures first, then return to the technical induction details. Also check the remark on the improved vanilla-GD learning-rate bound; it helps assess whether the analytical framework has broader value beyond the momentum case.

A careful read will likely take 1.5 to 2.5 hours. For readers focused on training stability and optimizer dynamics, this is worth reading with equations and figures side by side.1a5:T7f3,技术上分三层。第一层是机制定位。作者从 softmax backward 的标准形式 dS = P ⊙ (dP - δ) 出发，其中每一行的 δ_i = Σ_j P_ij dP_ij，本来保证 dS 每行求和为 0，这对应 softmax 对行平移不变。FP8 attention 的常见实现为了省算，会用保存下来的输出 O 来近似这个 row correction，即 δ_i^stale = <dO_i, Ô_i>。在高精度或前后向操作数一致时，这个捷径成立；但在 FP8 下，forward 用的是量化后的 P、V 得到 Ô，backward 又用重新量化后的 dO、V 得到 dP̂，两边的量化误差来源不同，导致 δ_i^stale 不再等于真正与 dP̂ 匹配的 correction。

第二层是误差如何影响训练。作者推导出 stale delta 会让 dS 的每一行出现非零残差 ε_i = Σ_j dS_ij^stale。这个残差不是无害的，因为它等价于在 matched gradient 上额外加了 ε_i P_ij 这一项。若 ε_i<0，会推动该行 logits 变尖；若 ε_i>0，会推动其变平。表面上看，不同行的残差可能互相抵消，但映射到 channel 维度后并不会自然抵消。作者观察到某些被“偏爱”的通道会持续受到同向压力，尤其体现在 key 侧 RMSNorm gain 被系统性推高，随后形成选择性放大，训练越久越明显。

第三层是修复方法 Delta-Matching。核心思想不是简单提高某个张量精度，而是让 backward row correction 使用与 backward 真实乘法路径一致的量。作者从未量化的 softmax 概率 P 和由 FP8 backward operands 在 FP32 中相乘得到的 dP̂ 出发，重新构造匹配的 δ，使 softmax gradient 的零行和不变量在给定数值假设下恢复。文中还特别说明，只把 dO 保留成 BF16 并不够，因为概率量化带来的不一致仍在。Delta-Matching 的价值在于它不依赖额外保存一个高精度 forward output，也不要求改 attention 结构；它针对的是 backward correction 这个具体失配点，因此可以直接嵌入 native block-scaled FP8 attention kernel。1a6:T822,实验设计比较扎实，重点不只是“最终分数更高”，而是把失效边界画出来了。首先在机制验证上，作者拿 1.67B GDN/GQA 训练末期 checkpoint 的 BF16 重算激活，去探测 FP8 kernel 在 6 个 attention layer、32 个训练窗口上的行为。结果显示，在 dS 量化之前，stale delta 造成的归一化 row-sum residual 中位数大约在 1.1e-2 到 4.7e-2，这已经不是可忽略的舍入噪声量级。

规模实验覆盖 569M、1.67B、5.29B。569M 上，stale-delta hybrid 只表现为较温和的 validation loss gap，下游任务大体还能保住；这解释了为什么一些早期工作在 sub-billion 规模上看起来“FP8 attention 也能训”。但到 1.67B 和 5.29B，训练前期还能跟住 BF16/FP32 mixed-precision reference，之后 loss 开始持续抬升，并带来下游性能下降，而且 5.29B 更早出现拐点，符合“误差积累且随规模加速”的判断。

作者还测试了多种可能的缓解手段。QK normalization 能减轻甚至避免某些配置下的灾难性崩溃，但仍留有明显性能差距；NoPE 在保留位置敏感 recurrent 层时只能延后退化；head dimension 从 128 提到 256 没有根治作用。这些结果说明问题不是某个架构细节偶然触发，而是 attention backward 数值约束被破坏后的普遍现象。

在架构泛化上，作者不只测标准 attention，还测了 Gated DeltaNet + MLA 的 hybrid，以及 KDA + GQA 的组合，stale-delta failure 都存在。在线性层精度、模型结构、训练阶段变化下，Delta-Matching 都能把训练 loss 和整体下游表现拉回到 BF16/FP32 mixed-precision attention reference 附近。

长上下文实验也很关键。按 Kimi K2 / DeepSeek-V3 风格 recipe，从 8K 扩到 64K，并把学习率降下来后，stale-delta baseline 相对 BF16/FP32 的 training-loss gap 要到大约 19k optimizer steps、约 20B tokens 后才超过 0.01。这个结果很有信息量：如果只做短程 context extension 验证，很容易误判为“方法没问题”。1a7:T7df,The technical story has three parts. First, the paper localizes the failure. Softmax backward has the form dS = P ⊙ (dP - δ), where δ_i = Σ_j P_ij dP_ij for each row. In exact arithmetic this guarantees that each row of dS sums to zero, reflecting softmax shift invariance. Many efficient implementations reuse the saved forward output O to compute the row correction, using δ_i^stale = <dO_i, O_hat_i>. This shortcut is valid when the forward and backward quantities are numerically consistent. Under FP8, however, O_hat comes from quantized forward operands, while dP_hat is formed from separately quantized backward operands. The two paths no longer match, so the shortcut becomes stale.

Second, the paper analyzes how this mismatch affects optimization. The stale correction induces a nonzero row residual ε_i = Σ_j dS_ij^stale. That residual adds an extra term ε_i P_ij to the matched gradient. Negative ε_i sharpens a row of logits; positive ε_i flattens it. Even if row-wise residuals nearly cancel globally, they do not cancel channel-wise after projection through Q/K/V. The authors show persistent pressure on selected channels, especially visible as systematic upward drift in key-side RMSNorm gains. This creates selective amplification over training rather than zero-mean noise.

Third, the proposed fix is Delta-Matching. The key idea is to compute the backward row correction from quantities that are actually consistent with the backward path: unquantized softmax probabilities P and FP32 products formed from the FP8 backward operands. Under the stated numerical assumptions, this restores the zero-row-sum invariant. The paper also shows that simply keeping dO in BF16 is insufficient, because the mismatch caused by probability quantization remains. Delta-Matching is attractive because it does not require storing an auxiliary high-precision forward output and does not depend on architectural changes. It directly patches the numerical inconsistency at the backward correction step.1a8:T81e,The experiments are strong because they map out the failure regime instead of only reporting end metrics. For mechanism validation, the authors probe the FP8 kernel using BF16-recomputed activations from final 1.67B GDN/GQA checkpoints, across six attention layers and 32 training windows. Before dS quantization, stale delta produces normalized row-sum residuals around 1.1e-2 to 4.7e-2 on average row medians over nonzero-gradient rows. That is far above negligible rounding noise.

The scale study covers 569M, 1.67B, and 5.29B models. At 569M, stale-delta hybrid training shows only a modest validation-loss gap and largely preserves downstream quality. This helps explain why earlier small-scale studies could appear encouraging. At 1.67B and 5.29B, however, stale-delta runs initially track BF16/FP32 references, then diverge later with rising loss and degraded downstream performance. The onset is earlier at 5.29B, consistent with cumulative error that accelerates with scale.

The paper also tests several mitigations. QK normalization can prevent catastrophic collapse in some settings, but it still leaves a substantial performance gap. NoPE delays degradation but does not remove it. Increasing head dimension from 128 to 256 does not solve the problem either. This is useful because it shows the issue is not an artifact of one architecture choice.

Generality is tested beyond a single attention design. The stale-delta failure appears in hybrids combining Gated DeltaNet with MLA, and KDA with GQA. Across architectures, training stages, and linear-layer precision settings, Delta-Matching recovers training loss and overall downstream performance close to BF16/FP32 mixed-precision attention references.

The long-context extension result is especially informative. Using a Kimi K2 / DeepSeek-V3 style recipe to extend from 8K to 64K with a lower learning rate, the stale-delta baseline does not exceed a 0.01 training-loss gap over BF16/FP32 until roughly 19k optimizer steps, about 20B tokens. This shows why short extension runs can miss the problem entirely.1a9:T559,Start with Sections 3.2 to 3.4. The main thing to understand is why the zero-row-sum property is not a cosmetic identity but the backward expression of softmax shift invariance, and why the saved-output shortcut breaks under FP8. Then read Figure 3 carefully. It is the bridge from local numerical inconsistency to long-horizon optimization damage, especially the channel-selective amplification story. After that, go to the scale and context-extension experiments in Section 4, focusing on the contrast between 569M, 1.67B, and 5.29B, and on the delayed failure during 8K to 64K extension.

Two details are worth extra attention. First, the paper shows that matching output-gradient precision alone is not enough. That is a broader lesson for low-precision training: local precision patches often fail if forward and backward are still inconsistent at the algorithmic level. Second, the mitigation results for QK norm and NoPE are useful because they separate error sensitivity from error source. They make training less fragile, but they do not repair the broken invariant.

For a fast read, spend most time on the derivation of stale delta, Figure 3, and the 1.67B main pretraining results. For implementation or reproduction, the appendices matter because the numerical assumptions and residual definitions are important to interpret the proof and the measurements.1aa:T8e9,实验部分信息量比较足，且不只停留在 ImageNet 分类。

1. 视觉监督训练：作者用约 1M 参数的 core 去初始化 85M 参数的 ViT-Base，再在 ImageNet-1K 上训练，top-1 相比随机初始化提升 +2.2 个百分点。这是最核心的 headline result，因为它说明一个很小的 recurrent core 可以迁移到大得多的目标模型，并带来稳定收益。

2. 下游表征质量：论文没有把收益局限在分类，而是检查了更能反映表征结构的任务。给出的数字包括：ADE20K 语义分割 mIoU 从 26.6 提升到 28.8；ImageNet-S 零样本分割 mAP 从 32.3 到 42.9；VOC07 目标定位 CorLoc 从 9.9 到 18.4；NYUv2 深度估计 RMSE 从 1.104 降到 0.998。这里的模式很重要：定位、分割、深度都变好，说明初始化影响的不只是分类头适配，而是中间表征更规整。

5. 机制分析：作者发现 recurrence 带来的参数共享会把计算分布到更广的方向集合，尤其包含低能量成分；在 ViT 中，结构主要集中在 attention value/output pathway，并能抑制高范数 token outlier。这个分析很关键，因为初始化论文常见问题是“有效但说不清为什么”，而这里至少给出了一条可检验的机制链路。

如果回到预训练视角，最值得核对的细节是：语言模型实验的规模、token 数、训练步数、与 procedural warm-up 本身相比的差距有多大，以及收益是否主要体现在早期收敛还是最终 loss 也持续更优。当前片段没有完整表格，这些数字需要看原文。1ab:T7c0,The method is called Procedural Core. It has two stages.

Stage one trains a very small recurrent auxiliary transformer on procedural data instead of warming up each target model directly. The auxiliary model is a minimal recurrent ViT with only three unique blocks: an input block, a recurrent middle block, and an output block. The objective and procedural data setup follow prior procedural warm-up work. The key idea is not to maximize the auxiliary model’s standalone performance, but to force useful computation into a compact reusable parameter set through depth-wise sharing. Recurrence acts as a compression mechanism: if deep transformers partly implement block-recurrent programs, then a recurrent model is a natural place to store that structure compactly.

Stage two expands this compact core into a target transformer of arbitrary width and depth. Depth is handled by unrolling the recurrent block across layers. Width is handled by tiling or expansion rules that map the smaller learned weights into a wider model. The result is a deterministic initialization procedure, not a new warm-up run for each target architecture.

The novelty has three layers. First, it turns procedural pretraining from a repeated training stage into a reusable initialization asset. Second, it uses recurrence as the transfer format, rather than directly interpolating or transplanting warm-up weights. Third, the paper goes beyond reporting gains and studies why the method transfers: depth-wise sharing appears to spread computation across a broader set of directions, including lower-energy components that matter for transfer; in ViTs, the strongest effects concentrate in the attention value/output pathway and suppress high-norm token outliers.

From an LLM perspective, the most interesting part is that the same idea is tested not only in vision but also in natural language and code modeling, which argues for a more general transformer prior rather than a vision-specific trick.1ac:T894,The experimental section is substantial and goes well beyond ImageNet classification.

1. Supervised vision training: a roughly 1M-parameter core is expanded to initialize an 85M-parameter ViT-Base, then trained on ImageNet-1K. This gives a +2.2 point top-1 improvement over random initialization. This is the central result because it shows that a very small recurrent core can transfer to a much larger target model.

2. Representation-sensitive downstream tasks: the gains are not limited to classification. Reported numbers include ADE20K semantic segmentation improving from 26.6 to 28.8 mIoU, ImageNet-S zero-shot segmentation from 32.3 to 42.9 mAP, VOC07 localization from 9.9 to 18.4 CorLoc, and NYUv2 depth estimation improving from 1.104 to 0.998 RMSE. This pattern matters: segmentation, localization, and depth all improve, which suggests the initialization changes internal representations rather than only helping classifier fitting.

3. Self-supervised and cross-domain transfer: the paper also reports gains for DINO, so the effect is not tied to supervised labels. More importantly, the method also helps language models trained on FineWeb-Edu and code models trained on CodeParrot. The excerpt does not expose exact language-model loss or perplexity numbers, but this is what separates the work from a standard CV initialization paper.

4. Baselines: Procedural Core beats both random initialization and structured initialization baselines such as Trockman and Kolter (2023). So the result is not just “any non-random start helps.”

5. Mechanistic analysis: the paper argues that recurrence spreads useful computation across a wider set of directions, especially lower-energy ones, and that in ViTs the effect concentrates in the attention value/output pathway while suppressing high-norm token outliers. This is important because initialization papers often stop at empirical gains; here there is at least a plausible mechanism to inspect.

For pretraining readers, the main missing details to verify in the full paper are the language-model scales, token budgets, training lengths, and how close this gets to running a full procedural warm-up directly on the target model.1ad:T60e,This deserves more than a quick skim if you care about initialization, data efficiency, procedural data, or the idea that pretraining effects might be compressible into a parameter prior. Start with the introduction and make the distinction from prior procedural warm-up work precise: the goal is not another warm-up stage, but a reusable core that captures its benefit.

Then read the method section carefully, especially the figure and the part describing the three unique blocks, recurrent training, and the expansion rules in depth and width. The key conceptual question is why recurrence should be a better carrier of transferable structure than simply training a small feed-forward transformer.

In the experiments, first read the ImageNet result, then the segmentation/localization/depth evaluations, because those are stronger evidence that the initialization changes representation quality. After that, check the language and code experiments to judge whether the method is truly transformer-general. Finally, read the mechanistic analysis around low-energy directions, the attention value/output pathway, and token-outlier suppression. That section is not the final word, but it gives concrete handles for follow-up work.

A focused read will take around 45 minutes. The most useful follow-up questions are: how the gains scale with model size, how much is lost relative to running a full procedural warm-up on the target model, and whether this initialization interacts with tokenizer choice, data curriculum, or training cooldown recipes.1ae:T981,技术核心是把当前层的 full weight gradient 分解成 LoRA 可访问部分和不可访问部分。对注入 LoRA 的线性层，设有效权重为 W_base + sBA。给定当前 batch 的输入激活 X 和反向信号 δ，完整权重梯度可恢复为 G_raw = δ^T X（按文中记号，batch 和 token 维展平后计算）。作者证明，由当前 A、B 的欧氏梯度所诱导出来的等价权重空间梯度，恰好张成当前 LoRA 参数化的 tangent space，也就是所谓 LoRA-accessible gradient space。于是可以把 G_raw 正交分解为切空间内的分量和法向分量；后者被称为 normal gradient。

这个 normal gradient 有两个关键性质。第一，只要它非零，取其负方向，在固定当前 adapter 与其他权重的局部条件下，是当前 batch loss 的下降方向。第二，它与当前 LoRA 一阶可达的所有方向都正交，因此不是通过改 adapter 学习率、初始化或梯度重标定就能补回来的。这也是作者为什么不继续做 LoRA factor 的优化修补，而是直接把 normal 分量用于更新 base weights。

GDLoRA 的实现分成两条支路：adapter branch 仍然是标准 LoRA + AdamW；normal branch 则从同一次前向/反向中恢复 full gradient，投影到当前切空间的正交补上，得到 normal gradient，然后直接更新 base weights。这里有两个实现细节值得注意。其一，作者只对 normal branch 做 token-count normalization，即按输入位置数归一化梯度幅值，保持方向不变，目的是让不同序列长度或 token 数下的 normal update 更稳定。其二，base weights 不维护额外的 momentum / variance buffer，也就是不用 Adam 状态去追踪这条支路，从而避免像 FFT 那样为全量参数付出 optimizer-state 内存。这样做的取舍很明确：用更“轻”的 base update 换取部分 full-gradient 信息，而不是完全复制 FFT 的优化器行为。

和已有方法相比，差异也很清楚。Fira 试图用低秩投影近似 full-rank adaptive update，但需要周期性 SVD 或复用投影基，存在梯度子空间漂移问题。LoRA-GA、LoRA-Pro 则仍停留在 adapter 参数化内部，改善的是 LoRA 所诱导的权重梯度与 full gradient 的对齐程度。GDLoRA 直接承认当前 LoRA 切空间之外还有信息，并显式抽取这部分正交分量来更新 base weights，因此方法逻辑更直接。1af:T95c,The method starts from a LoRA-injected linear layer with effective weight W_base + sBA. Given forward activations X and backward signals delta for the current batch, the unconstrained full weight gradient can be reconstructed as G_raw = delta^T X after flattening batch and token dimensions. The key theoretical result is that the set of equivalent weight-space gradients induced by Euclidean gradients on A and B coincides exactly with the tangent space of the current LoRA parameterization. This defines the LoRA-accessible gradient space.

Once this space is characterized, the full gradient can be orthogonally decomposed into a tangent component and a normal component. The latter is called the normal gradient. This component has two important properties. First, when nonzero, its negative is a local descent direction for the current batch loss when the current adapters and other parameters are held fixed. Second, it is orthogonal to every first-order direction available through the current LoRA factors, so it cannot be recovered merely by better initialization, rescaling, or re-optimizing the adapter gradients within the same parameterization.

GDLoRA uses two update branches. The adapter branch is standard LoRA optimized with AdamW. The normal branch reconstructs the full gradient from the same forward/backward pass, projects out the tangent-space component, and directly applies the remaining normal gradient to the base weights. A notable design choice is that token-count normalization is applied only to the normal branch, to stabilize update magnitude across different numbers of input positions while preserving direction. Another important choice is that the base weights do not maintain additional momentum or variance buffers. This is how the method avoids the optimizer-state overhead of FFT. In effect, GDLoRA supplements LoRA with a lightweight base-weight update that carries information unavailable to the current low-rank factors.

Compared with prior work, the distinction is clear. Fira approximates full-rank adaptive updates through projected gradients and periodically refreshed low-rank bases, which introduces basis-refresh trade-offs. LoRA-GA and LoRA-Pro improve how adapter gradients approximate the full gradient, but still remain inside the LoRA-induced update space. GDLoRA instead explicitly extracts the orthogonal complement and uses it directly.1b0:T5a4,The experiments span natural language understanding, mathematical and commonsense reasoning, and image classification. The main empirical claim is that under matched adapter and optimizer configurations, GDLoRA improves average performance by about 2% to 4% over standard LoRA and often approaches, or in some settings matches, full fine-tuning.

The emphasis on matched configurations matters. The paper is not claiming gains from extra trainable parameters or full optimizer states. It is testing whether the normal-gradient branch consistently adds useful information beyond what LoRA can express at first order. The most informative comparisons are therefore against standard LoRA, FFT, and methods such as Fira, LoRA-GA, and LoRA-Pro.

The ablations to pay attention to are the ones that isolate the mechanism: whether token-count normalization is necessary for the normal branch; how much is gained by combining LoRA updates with normal base-weight updates versus using either alone; how the method behaves at different ranks; and whether the benefit shrinks as rank increases. If the paper’s interpretation is correct, the gain should be more pronounced at lower ranks, where the LoRA tangent space is narrower and the normal component is more likely to contain important descent directions.

This is not a large-scale scaling-law paper. The value lies in making the missing-gradient story concrete, measurable, and empirically useful.1b1:T4e1,Read this paper with one question in mind: is LoRA limited mainly by low-rank capacity, or by the restricted first-order update space of its current parameterization? Start with the introduction and the theorem-level characterization that the accessible gradient space equals the tangent space. That is the conceptual center of the paper. Then read the definition and properties of the normal gradient carefully, especially why it is a local descent direction and why it cannot be represented by first-order perturbations of the current LoRA factors.

After that, inspect the algorithm section to see that GDLoRA reuses signals already available from a standard backward pass rather than introducing an expensive second-order or repeatedly decomposed procedure. In the experiments, focus on the main comparison tables against LoRA and FFT, then the comparisons with Fira, LoRA-GA, and LoRA-Pro, and finally the ablations on token normalization, rank, and base-weight update design.

A 30-minute read is enough to capture the main idea. If you want to judge whether it is practical for large-model training, spend extra time on the appendix details about compute overhead, memory accounting, and how full-gradient recovery is implemented in practice.1b2:T43d,The analysis is built around preconditioned SGD with a fixed positive-definite preconditioner, which makes the theory broad enough to cover simplified versions of SGD, AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam-like methods. For the early phase, the paper uses Lyapunov stability analysis to connect stable step size with local sharpness. Since early pre-training lies in a highly sharp region, a large learning rate before sufficient warmup violates the stability condition. This explains why warmup is not just a smoothing heuristic but a way to wait until the landscape becomes less sharp. For the late phase, the loss is locally approximated by a quadratic around a minimum, and the stochastic dynamics are analyzed under gradient noise. The resulting depth-flatness trade-off says that lower noise emphasizes loss minimization and produces deeper minima, while higher noise regularizes sharpness and pushes toward wider basins. Because the theory identifies η/B as the relevant noise-scale term, increasing batch size and decaying learning rate become two related ways of reducing stochasticity.1b3:T437,The main experiments use LLaMA-2 style models with 93M and 170M parameters, trained on FineWeb-Edu with context length 1024. Training budgets range from 50 to 1000 tokens per parameter. The optimizer is AdamW with β1=0.95, β2=0.95, weight decay 0.1, and gradient clipping at 1.0. Evaluation uses a held-out validation split of about 50M tokens. The empirical results support three claims. First, local sharpness is very high at the start of pre-training and then drops, matching the sharp-to-flat picture. Large peak learning rates without enough warmup lead to loss spikes or plateaus. Second, larger peak learning rates require proportionally longer warmup within the tested regime. Third, batch size controls the late-stage noise scale: smaller batches lead to wider basins, larger batches to deeper ones, and batch-size ramping can maintain steady loss reduction with fewer consumed tokens. The comparison between batch-size ramping and learning-rate decay supports the η/B interpretation, as both reduce the effective noise scale and can yield similar performance trends.1b4:T4e3,The work defines a use as one gradient computation reading a rounded tensor. A backward-state policy assigns a value to every such use. The reference is the gradient of the computation that actually produced the loss, with rounding handled by a straight-through convention. Under this reference, each use must read the value used by the corresponding forward operation, or a substitute that gives the same gradient in expectation conditional on the realized forward computation and the incoming gradient received by that use. This conditional requirement is the crucial step: an incoming gradient may depend on the realized rounding, so two values sampled from the same rounding distribution need not be interchangeable. The attention correction term D = rowsum(dO ∘ O) is used as the main example. If dO depends on the forward rounding of O, then reusing that rounded O and drawing a fresh rounding from the same distribution can produce different training behavior. The paper also shows that one tensor can require different values for different gradients, for example in normalization and in rounded attention probabilities. The proposed per-use requirements are then checked with an executable finite-case checker for concrete operator policies.1b5:T4b5,The experiments are built around 390M-parameter training runs and low-precision attention backward. In the FOG 390M setting, NVIDIA Transformer Engine FP8 attention fails in all three seeds tested. Replacing only the backward with BF16 while keeping the FP8 forward removes the failure, isolating the issue to the backward policy. In paired runs with an emulated FP8 attention backward, the forward randomly rounds the attention output O. Training fails when the D term reuses the forward-rounded O, but succeeds when D reads a fresh rounding from the same distribution; this is repeated in three paired 390M runs. The two choices have the same copy accuracy, so the difference comes from the dependency between the realized rounding and dO. Another experiment shows that final loss is not enough: a policy that lets the next layer consume the rounded output while both gradients read the original can end with loss inside a pre-specified margin of the reference policy, even though it violates the per-use reference. Predictions about reuse effects are also registered and tested on three PyTorch and Transformer Engine operators, and all predictions match, including cases where reuse should not matter.1b6:T880,The paper has two technical pillars: a lower-bound construction and matching upper-bound analysis. The lower bound is the conceptual center. The authors build a rank-one gradient example with unequal row magnitudes. In that setting, Muon’s polar-factor update remains well aligned with the gradient, whereas NorMuon’s row-wise renormalization equalizes row magnitudes but rotates the update away from the gradient. That is the key mechanism: better neuron-wise balance can come with worse descent alignment. The authors then embed this mechanism into a smooth objective whose gradient stays effectively constant along the iterate path, isolating the directional distortion caused by row normalization from other training effects. This yields an algorithm-dependent lower bound of Ω(mLε^-2) iterations for NorMuon to reach an ε-stationary point, compared with Muon’s O(Lε^-2) rate in the same geometry.

The upper-bound side shows the m factor is not merely a proof artifact. The paper proves O(mLε^-2) in the deterministic setting and O(mLε^-2 + m^2Lσ^2ε^-4) in the stochastic setting, with noise measured through a nuclear-norm variance bound. Importantly, the analysis explicitly accommodates approximate polar computation and fixed-parameter EMA momentum. Even with exact polar computation and arbitrary fixed momentum parameters, the dimension-dependent penalty remains. That makes the result structurally stronger: the slowdown is tied to the normalization step itself.

Relative to prior work, the distinction is sharp. NorMuon motivated row normalization through neuron-wise balancing and mitigation of low-leverage rows receiving persistently tiny updates. This paper does not dispute that empirical mechanism. Instead, it shows that balancing update magnitudes and improving convergence are different objectives. The analysis shifts attention from per-row magnitude fairness to update-gradient alignment under operator-norm geometry. That framing is also useful when comparing related variants such as Muon+, MuonEq, and other matrix-aware optimizers: are they changing update magnitudes, update directions, or both, and what is the cost of each choice?1b7:T5b5,The experiments are designed to expose the theory–practice gap rather than to maximize benchmark coverage. There are two main parts. First, synthetic optimization problems reproduce the theoretical mechanism: on controlled tasks aligned with the lower-bound construction, NorMuon is slower than Muon, confirming that row normalization can indeed hurt optimization speed when directional distortion dominates. Second, in LLM pretraining, NorMuon outperforms Muon. That contrast is the puzzle highlighted by the title.

The most important empirical takeaway is therefore not a single headline number but the coexistence of three facts: the worst-case complexity of NorMuon carries an extra m factor; this penalty is visible on synthetic tasks; and NorMuon can still be better in realistic pretraining. That strongly suggests its practical gains come from training-specific effects such as improved neuron activity balance or better interaction with real gradient statistics, not from a uniformly better smooth-optimization rate.

The explicit quantitative results stated in the paper include: a lower bound of Ω(mLε^-2) for NorMuon, a deterministic upper bound of O(mLε^-2), a stochastic upper bound of O(mLε^-2 + m^2Lσ^2ε^-4), and Muon’s comparison rate of O(Lε^-2). The provided full-content excerpt does not include detailed pretraining-scale numbers such as model size, token count, or exact validation-loss deltas, so those should not be inferred.1b8:T4d8,If reading selectively, start with the introduction’s claim that balanced neuron updates do not imply faster convergence. That is the right lens for the whole paper. Then go to the lower-bound section and study the rank-one unequal-row construction carefully. The key idea is not complicated once isolated: row normalization fixes row imbalance but weakens gradient alignment. Also pay attention to how the authors embed this into a smooth objective with nearly constant gradients along the trajectory; that is what turns an intuitive geometric observation into a rigorous lower bound.

After that, read the experimental comparison between synthetic tasks and LLM pretraining. The paper is strongest when read as an explanation of why both results can be true at once. For deeper study, focus on three questions: what properties of real LLM gradients make row normalization beneficial despite the worst-case penalty; whether the m factor is sensitive to width, sparsity, or training schedule; and whether one could design conditional or selective row normalization that activates only when low-leverage rows are actually suppressed. A quick skim takes 30–45 minutes. A careful read of the proofs and appendices likely needs 2–3 hours.1b9:T4e8,The paper uses Partial Information Decomposition to separate multimodal information into four channels. Redundant information R is accessible from either modality. Unique information U_1 and U_2 is accessible only from modality 1 or modality 2. Synergistic information S is accessible only when both modalities are present together. The proposed scaling law writes data loss as a sum of four independent power-law curves. Each curve receives only the relevant data stream: R can be reduced by either modality, U_1 by modality 1 data, U_2 by modality 2 data, and S only by the paired count n_p. This differs from prior L(N, D_1, D_2) forms because it gives paired data its own causal role rather than folding it into modality counts. The experimental protocol is built to isolate this variable. Unpaired examples are represented by a learnable null vector plus a modality-presence bit. At test time, both modalities are always present. Cross-entropy is the main loss, with accuracy checked separately. The main sweeps fix architecture and parameter count, folding finite-model effects into E_N, while appendices repeat Digits and VQA under different architectures and parameter sizes to check that the qualitative conclusions are not tied to a single model.1ba:T5ca,The paper evaluates three settings. Digits combines MNIST images and AudioMNIST spectrograms in a four-digit classification task where the four positions correspond to U_1, U_2, R, and S, giving explicit control over the information channels. VQA trains classification heads on top of frozen pretrained embeddings; this setting is dominated by the text modality and is useful for observing how unpaired data helps non-synergistic information. NLVR2 finetunes a pretrained multimodal transformer on a task where mutual information is largely synergistic and unimodal models remain near chance. Across settings, the authors sweep total data D, compute budget C, paired count n_p, and multiple random seeds. They count D as D_1 + D_2, the sum of unique examples per modality. As p approaches 1, the number of unique rows decreases; training steps are fixed, so fully paired data sees more epochs but the same number of gradient updates. This counting convention favors unpaired data, making improvements from higher p more attributable to pairing itself. The main findings are consistent: pairing ratio has a large effect on loss; laws without p cannot capture the observed curves; only paired data reduces synergistic loss; unpaired data reduces redundant or unimodal loss only up to the relevant floors; and synergy shows a threshold-like acquisition pattern. The provided text does not include exact fit-error numbers for the proposed law, so no additional numeric claims are added.1bb:T42e,The authors study an online teacher-student model with a single softmax layer trained by cross-entropy. Inputs are sampled from an isotropic Gaussian and RMS-normalized, mirroring hidden states before an LM head. A fixed teacher matrix produces hard one-hot labels from the argmax of its softmax output. The student learns with different optimizers. The setup preserves the key nonlinearity behind peaked distribution learning: reducing loss requires both growing the student weight norm, which sharpens the output distribution, and aligning the student direction with the teacher. The analysis decomposes the loss into a radial channel, controlled by norm growth and softmax saturation, and a tangential channel, controlled by directional misalignment. These channels decay with exponents α_r and α_t. SGD places both near one third. Adam produces a different dynamic regime, with α_r near one half and α_t near zero. Across seven optimizers, the exponents obey the relation 2α_r + α_t = 1, which yields the same tuned data scaling L*(D) proportional to D^{-1/3}.1bc:T597,The setup treats a benchmark as a fixed list of M questions. For each question, generated answers have a verifier score S and a correctness bit Y. At budget k, the selected answer is the one with the highest verifier score among k samples, and the curve reports the average correctness over the fixed question list. The audit may adaptively choose questions, extend answer paths, query correctness labels, and stop when it can return a simultaneous confidence band with half-width ε and failure probability δ. The analysis counts three resources: generated answers, correctness queries, and question visits. For a fixed list, the main cost law for certifying all budgets up to K is, up to logarithmic factors, K/ε + min(M, ε^{-2}) + s/ε^2. The three terms correspond to rare high-scoring answers at large budgets, the identity of the benchmark questions, and within-question variance accumulated along the curve. Matching lower bounds show that these terms are intrinsic. A key technical device is a coupling of nested winners on one answer path, which lets a single path serve all budgets. The practical algorithm is a paired audit: each round draws two fresh paths per question, uses an exponential inequality for paired Bernoulli draws to build anytime-valid simultaneous bands, and then applies a corrected exact-binomial final look to stop at a fixed round. Combined with a multilevel audit, it attains near-minimax cost.1bd:T45b,The empirical study uses 185 held-out score pools. The curves often plateau early: the median curve is within 1/32 of its best value by k=10, so small differences matter. On 100 MMLU-Pro questions, a fixed exact-binomial design needs 192,000 generated answers to certify all budgets up to K=64 within ±1/32 at 95% confidence. By contrast, one path of 64 answers per question uses only 6,400 answers and gives unbiased estimates of all points, but does not provide a sufficiently tight simultaneous guarantee. At budget 64, roughly three quarters of the variance in selected-answer correctness comes from between-question variation, which explains why balanced revisits to every fixed question can save cost. In experiments, the paired audit uses 0.74, 0.66, and 0.53 times the generated answers of the cheapest competing certified audit at K=64, 256, and 1024. It is cheaper on all eight generator-benchmark answer sets, misses none of 3,255 runs against exact curves, and its cost follows the three-term theory closely with R^2=0.995. Nonnegative prices on token occurrences yield a lower bound through shortest paths and vocabulary-budget selection; maximising over all prices recovers the linear programming relaxation, and an inde","starred":false,"priority":"p2","reading_tier":"skim","source":"arxiv","sources":["arxiv"],"published_at":"","category_id":"pretraining_data","cover_url":"/covers/2609_35869.png","hf_upvotes":0,"arxiv_categories":["cs.AI","cs.CL"],"summary":{"core_problem":"这篇工作讨论的是 tokenizer 里一个常被混在一起、但其实应当分开看的问题：预分词边界（通常由 regex 决定）到底让最优压缩损失了多少。过去很多工作会在“固定边界约束”下比较不同词表学习算法，然后得出 BPE 已经接近最优之类的结论；但这种结论只在受限可行域内成立，不能回答“如果允许 token 跨词边界，理论上还能少多少 token”。作者要解决的核心问题，就是给这个边界约束本身做一个可验证的、双边夹逼的压缩证书，而不是只比较某个具体 tokenizer 的经验结果。","importance":"对预训练研究的意义主要有两层。第一，它把 tokenizer 研究里“词表学习算法是否接近最优”和“边界约束本身值不值得保留”这两个问题拆开了。这个拆分很重要，因为很多关于 BPE、Unigram、无边界 tokenizer 的争论，实际是在比较不同优化问题。第二，它给出了一个可以独立验证的下界证书，使得“boundary tax”不再只是经验观察，而是有明确数值区间的优化量。对基座预训练来说，这直接关系到序列长度、训练 FLOPs、上下文利用率，以及 tokenizer 设计时压缩率和预测难度之间的取舍。论文后半部分又进一步说明：更短的 token 序列并不自动带来更好的 held-out 预测，这对“只看 token count 优化 tokenizer”是一个明确的纠偏。","technical_approach":"方法上，作者把最小 token 数分词写成一个带词表预算的整数规划。语料被表示成字节级 DAG：节点是字节位置，边是候选 substring 的出现位置；字节边永远可用，多字节边只有当对应字符串被选入词表时才可用。给定词表后，每个文档的最小 token 分词就是这个 DAG 上的最短路。难点在于，一个词表项一旦被选中，会同时激活它在全语料中的所有 occurrence，因此词表选择和具体分词路径是耦合的。\n\n作者的关键技巧是做 occurrence-level 的拉格朗日松弛：给每个候选 occurrence 一个非负价格 λ_e。这样，文档侧变成“带价格的最短路”，词表侧变成“收集某个 token 在所有 occurrence 上的总 bid”，再减去预算 K 下 top-K bid 的总和，就得到一个全局下界。这个形式有几个优点：一是不需要通用 LP 求解器，核心计算退化为每篇文档的 shortest path 加上全局 token bid 排序；二是价格可以近似优化，但证书有效性可以用独立的整数检查器验证；三是它既适用于 regex-constrained 语料，也适用于 unrestricted 语料，因此可以直接比较两种最优值，定义 boundary tax。\n\n除了两端点，作者还引入 boundary licence：允许有限数量的词表项跨越 regex cut。这样可以在“完全受限”和“完全无边界”之间画出压缩前沿，测量少量跨边界 token 到底能回收多少压缩收益。这一点比单纯比较两个端点更有分析价值，因为它把问题从二元选择变成了预算分配问题。\n\n论文还把压缩和预测分开评估。压缩侧看最优 token count 及其证书区间；预测侧则在明确的 vocabulary 和 decoder protocol 下做 held-out bits-per-byte 比较。作者强调，最小 token 数只是一个分词目标，不等于语言建模目标；无边界词表会改变 token 频率分布、上下文粒度和可预测性，因此需要单独测。","experiments":"核心结果有三组。第一，在 English Wikipedia 上，作者给出边界税的证书区间：regex 边界使最优 token 数增加 28.3% 到 36.8%。这个量级不小，说明预分词边界不是一个轻微工程细节，而是显著限制了压缩最优值。第二，BPE 相对“受边界约束的理论下界”只高 2.1%，说明在固定 regex 约束下，BPE 的压缩效率确实已经接近最优；但相对“无边界的理论下界”则高 10.9%，说明如果把问题定义改掉，BPE 离真正的全局最优并不近。这个结果很好地解释了为什么一边有人说 BPE 已经够好，另一边又有人通过放松边界拿到明显更短序列：他们比较的不是同一个 optimum。\n\n第三，作者做了 12 种语言的配对实验。结论是：无边界拟合出来的词典在压缩上更好，但测试集平均 bits per byte 在每种语言上都更高；用独立调参种子和评测种子复现实验后，这个方向在 12 种语言里保留了 11 种。也就是说，跨边界 token 虽然减少了步数，却往往让预测更难。论文把这点解释为词表内容、token 频率和有效字节上下文同时发生了变化。若从 LM 训练角度看，这意味着“更短序列”并不等于“更低 NLL”，甚至可能相反。\n\n从消融角度，boundary licence It is a useful design point for latent reasoning and recurrent language modeling: keep the standard next-token objective, but add a supervised latent feedback channel that the model can consume at the next step.","technical_approach":"LIFT turns recurrent-state learning into a teacher-forced prediction problem. During training, each position receives both a token x_i and a state s_i, and the model is trained to predict the next token x_{i+1} and the next state s_{i+1}. The states are derived from the next-token distributions of an external pretrained teacher model. The teacher is used to supply informative input states during training, not merely soft targets for distillation. At inference time, the teacher is removed and the model feeds back its own predicted states. This differs from sequential latent-rollout methods, which are expensive to train, and from Jacobi-style feedback approximations, which require multiple parallel refinement iterations and therefore trade quality against training cost.","experiments":"The paper reports both controlled synthetic experiments and language-model pretraining runs. Many deployment tasks can be formulated as sampling from a tilted version of the pretrained distribution, such as reward-guided generation, posterior sampling, constrained generation, and reasoning-time selection. Feynman–Kac SMC is exact in principle, but in practice its weights often collapse when the proposal dynamics are poorly aligned with the tilt, so additional particles do not translate into proportional gains.","importance":"The main relevance for pretraining research is in the inference interface of non-autoregressive language modeling. Its contribution is to give a discrete counterpart of DriftLite: an exact way to move correction mass between proposal jump rates and residual Feynman–Kac weights while preserving the target tilted path. This is useful for diffusion LM research because it provides a principled route to combine pretrained DLMs with rewards, constraints, verifiers, or posterior signals without introducing an additional training stage.","technical_approach":"The method represents the reverse process of a discrete diffusion model as a continuous-time Markov chain over a finite state space. The pretrained reverse rates define a sparse directed graph of allowed transitions. FluxLite shows that any sparse perturbation of these jump rates can be exactly compensated by a q_t-weighted graph-divergence correction in the Feynman–Kac potential. The target path distribution is unchanged, but the residual reweighting variance can be reduced. This turns proposal design into sparse graph-flux variance minimization. The paper instantiates the framework with a one-hop local heuristic, HEU, and a quadratic-programming method over a pretrained-rate basis, D-VCG. samplers。结论是，Fork-dLLM 的 pass@k scaling 可以匹配 AR sampling，但所需 NFEs 只有后者的约 1/2 到 1/3，也就是 2–3× 更省。这个结果很关键，因为它说明“避免 flexibility trap”并不需要把 dLLM 退化成全 AR。论文还进一步表明，经过适当调参，其他 confidence-based samplers 也能在远低于 t","starred":false,"priority":"p2","reading_tier":"skim","source":"arxiv","sources":["arxiv"],"published_at":"","category_id":"architecture","cover_url":"/covers/2609_39560.png","hf_upvotes":0,"arxiv_categories":["cs.LG"],"summary":{"core_problem":"这篇论文解决的是 workload、硬件和质量口径下评估。","experiments":"论文给出的关键数字很有用。Llama-3-70B 在 BF16 下权重约 140 GB，已经超过单张 80 GB HBM 加速卡容量。其 KV cache 公式为 Bkv = 2·L·nkv·dh·wkv·s。对 Llama-3-70B，L=80、nkv=8、dh=128、BF16 每元素 2 字节，因此每 token KV cache 为 327,680 字节。单条 128k-token 序列会额外产生约 42 GB KV state；到 10^6 tokens 时约为 328 GB，相当于超过四张 H100 80GB 的总 HBM。算力利用侧，BF16 decode 的权重读取 intensity 约 1 FLOP/B，而 H100 ridge point 约 295 FLOP/B；GQA 即使 group factor 为 8，attention-side intensity 也只有约 8 FLOP/B。batching 的分界也被明确量化：权重侧 intensity 随 batch size 线性上升，H100 BF16 下接近 ridge 需要 batch size 约 295；KV 侧 intensity 不随 batch size 改善。论文的实验价值不在提出新 kernel，而在把各类 上，而是记录“已完成的 branch subgraph + 触发它的输入 + 它读过的外部依赖”。后续请求只有在输入精确匹配、且这些外部 reads 仍然新鲜时，才能消费该结果；一旦相关外部状态发生写入，就失效。这解决了 agent 工作流里 retrieval/tool 结果依赖外部环境、不能只靠 prompt exact match 复用的问题。\n\n第二层是 unresolved Three constraints must hold together: the reusable unit is an internal subgraph rather than a whole request; the key that authorizes reuse does not exist until the branch resolves, yet work should begin during that waiting window; and speculative execution must be priced against online serving load, otherwise a strategy that helps at low load can hurt under contention.","importance":"This is not a pretraining paper, but it is a meaningful serving paper for agent-native LLM systems. low-bit quantization of recurrent states in hybrid language models. Unlike ordinary activations or KV entries, errors in recurrent states persist and affect future readouts. Channels with slow decay retain quantization noise for many steps, while fast-decaying channels dissipate it quickly. Uniform range-based quantization therefore allocates precision without considering the future impact of the error.","importance":"The main value for pretraining and architecture work is the connection between hybrid-LM state dynamics and inference-time memory efficiency. Models such as Kimi Delta Attention, Gated DeltaNet, and Mamba-2 replace part of the attention cache with fixed-size recurrent states, shifting the systems bottleneck toward state storage, read/write bandwidth, and numerical precision. The paper provides a data-free, training-free, rotation-free allocation rule for recurrent-state quantization. It also makes a broader point: KV-cache quantization heuristics are not directly sufficient for recurrent architectures, because state errors have temporal dynamics. This can inform future choices of decay parameterization, state grouping, normalization, and quantization-friendly architecture design.","technical_approach":"The method assigns a distortion weight to each state channel using an observability Gramian. Under a local linear noise model, steady-state readout MSE can be approximated as sum_i Gamma_i sigma_i^2, where sigma_i^2 is the quantization noise variance for a row and Gamma_i measures how strongly that row’s error will be observed in future outputs. For diagonal decay without erasure, the paper derives Gamma_i = rho_i / (C expm1(2 s_i)), where s_i is the decay rate, rho_i is query-weighted energy, and C is the write-back interval. Slow decay therefore receives higher precision. These weights are combined with normalized state ranges inside output-normalization groups and plugged into a classical high-rate mixed-precision bit-allocation rule. Decay rates are quantized uniformly in log s, reflecting the sensitivity of long time constants to small relative changes in decay.","experiments":"The experiments evaluate three hybrid models and seven baselines. With per-token recurrent-state quantization, a 4-bit mean payload reduces excess negative log-likelihood by factors of 3.3 to 27.9 relative to the best baseline. At 6 bits, the NLL gap to the FP32-state baseline is below 0.005 nats. The paper includes ablations separating the contributions of variable bit widths, decay-aware weighting, range normalization, and logarithmic decay-rate quantization. It also reports an important caveat: deterministic rounding at C=1 can create correlated errors. In simulations using Kimi-like decays and rank-one writes, lag-one error correlations reach 0.23 for very slow channels, and three-to-five-bit readout error can range from 0.17x to 2.4x the independent-noise prediction. By six bits, discrepancies are typically within 20%. This avoids token-level deletion that can break tool calls, code, or execution logs. The objective is connected to an Information Bottleneck formulation: retain as little history as possible while preserving information predictive of future actions. Direct optimization is intractable because it requires searching over subsets of spans and evaluating distributions over future trajectories. FOCUS approximates span utility at test time through Monte Carlo rollouts: remove or perturb a span, generate future plans, and measure whether the predicted decision trajectory changes. A verification step is added to recover critical spans that stochastic plan-based estimation may miss. That framing is relevant to distillation, RL post-training, synthetic data filtering, and long-chain reasoning stability. It first rolls out the current quantized policy and collects the states actually visited at deployment time. At each shared quantized prefix, both the dense model and the quantized model are queried, which isolates next-token decision changes at the same state. The method then identifies mismatches and near-miss decision boundaries, runs short counterfactual rollouts from competing tokens, and estimates how far the resulting futures separate. Boundary erosion, same-state distribution discrepancy, and branch consequence are combined into a Decision-Consequence risk used to weight calibration. A static context anchor is kept to preserve broader multimodal behavior. After each calibration update, trajectories are refreshed under the updated quantized policy. The paper also derives a bound that decomposes behavioral deviation into current policy discrepancy and the future value span conditioned on alternative actions.","experiments":"The experiments cover multiple VLM backbones and quantization settings. Calibrating on quantized-policy states reduces on-policy divergence by 30.8% for QIG and 43.3% for MASQuant compared with static-state calibration. 级别不加载某些专家，输出会发生变化。论文把某个专家被移除造成的层输出误差写成平方范数形式，其中既包含单专家 removal term，也包含多个被同时移除时的 cross terms。作者的关键判断是：在实际选择中，忽略 cross terms 仍能较稳定地得到接近最优的 batch expert set，因此可以把每个专家的贡献独立打分，再在固定预算下保留分数最高的专家。\n\n具体分数来自“预测的移除误差”。对某个 token-专家对，若移除专家 u，误差近似与 router weight 的平方以及该专家输出能量 ||E_u(z_t)||^2 相关。难点在于真正的 expert output 只有把专家权重取回并执行后才知道，而 batch 选择恰恰发生在此之前。BASE
